#6598. I Tried Keurig’s First-Ever Espresso Machine—Is It Worth Adding To Your Coffee Routine?

I’ve owned a Keurig, I’ve owned a Nespresso, and I’ve spent way too much money on coffee shop runs in between. Needless to say, I’m an expert on the subject. So when I heard that Keurig was launching its first-ever espresso machine, my interest was piqued. Could the brand that turned single-serve coffee into the household standard successfully switch up its game?

Keurig’s latest and possibly greatest innovation—a two-in-one single-serve coffee maker and espresso machine called the Alta System—will turn your home kitchen into a coffee shop thanks to a multifunctional design that brews everything from regular coffee to espresso, cappuccinos, and lattes. It comes with a built-in milk frother and functions exclusively on the new plastic- and aluminum-free pods (sustainability, hallelujah!).

Here’s whether the Keurig Alta System lives up to the hype, how it compares to other machines, and whether it deserves a spot on your own kitchen coffee bar.

Let’s go a little more in-depth, shall we? The Keurig Alta System is the brand’s new single-serve coffee and espresso machine that does a lot more than your standard K-Cup brewer. Unlike the brand’s traditional lineup, which uses K-Cup pods, the Alta introduces an entirely new innovation: AltaRounds. Your machine can read a code on the AltaRounds and adjust its brew settings accordingly, whether that’s pressure, temperature, or the water-to-coffee ratio. (K-Cups are still compatible with the Alta).

The integrated milk frother is another major upgrade for Keurig, letting you make hot and cold foam.

The Keurig Alta System is $499.99, which, yes, is pricier than other Keurig models. However, classic espresso machines can run you upwards of $1,000.

As for the AltaRounds, they’re sold in boxes of eight, ranging from $9.99 to $10.99 depending on the variety. If you wanna break that up by coffee, it’s about $1.25 to $1.37 a cup. Not too shabby.

As someone who is impatient and terrible at reading directions (hello, your type B friend reporting for duty), I wasn’t overly optimistic I’d figure it out that quickly. But it’s actually an easy device to navigate, thanks to the convenient LED screen that walks you through the whole process.

I was immediately transfixed by the machine. I texted my boyfriend, “I’m in love with it,” before it even finished brewing my first coffee. The Alta feels so much chicer on my countertops, and the pods are smaller and store more easily. Once I finally took that first sip, I was ready to toss my old Keurig in the trash (respectfully).

The drip coffee and espresso shots taste like something straight from an award-winning barista. I love the flexibility to make a black coffee one day and an iced caramel latte the next. And the milk frother just takes the entire thing to the next level.

Listen, $500 for a coffee machine is a lot. And maybe because of that, this isn’t an upgrade you can make immediately. Still, the Keurig Alta System is worth the hype; if you can swap your classic single-serve maker for it, you should. It checks literally every box—it’s more aesthetic, more versatile, and more sustainable.

The only caveat is if you’re the type of person who exclusively drinks drip coffee. In that case, it might not be worth the splurge. But if you want to cosplay as a barista and whip up new creations, from frothy cappuccinos to iced lattes and espresso martinis, the Alta provides all the room to experiment (and it will ultimately save you money on those $10 coffee runs).

#6597. Mussels With Garlicky Miso Broth

Mussels deserve your attention on weeknights. An affordable and accessible protein, they also happen to cook in less time than it takes to boil water. As the bivalves steam, they release a briny liquid, further perfuming the buttery, sake-fortified miso broth. Load up each bowl with a few good ladles, slurping every drop with an assist from crusty bread or warm rice. And why not enjoy the rest of the bottle of sake alongside your meal?

The seafood counter at your supermarket should sell rinsed and debarred mussels, but it’s easy to do at home. Discard any with cracked shells. Gently tap open raw mussels on a counter to see if they slowly close; if they do, those are okay to use. Swish them in a water-filled salad spinner or colander fitted inside a bowl, draining and refilling until water runs clear (give any especially dirty ones a scrub with a sponge). Use a towel to pull off the fibrous beard and set on a towel-lined tray in the fridge until you’re ready to cook.

More seafood dinners this way: Avgolemono Seafood Stew; Spaghetti alle Vongole; and Gorgeous Green Shrimp.

Place 2 Tbsp. scallions from 8 scallions, thinly sliced on a diagonal, in a small bowl and set aside for serving.

Melt 6 Tbsp. unsalted butter in a large pot over medium heat. Add 8 garlic cloves, thinly sliced, and remaining scallions to pot and cook, stirring often, until softened, about 4 minutes. Add 2 Tbsp. white miso paste and ½ tsp. crushed red pepper flakes (if using) and cook until miso is broken up and incorporated into butter, about 20 seconds. Pour in 1 cup dry sake or dry white wine and stir to combine, then add 3–3½ lb. mussels, scrubbed, debearded. Cover pot and increase heat to medium-high. Cook, shaking pot occasionally, until mussels open, 5–7 minutes (discard any that do not open). Remove pot from heat.

Squeeze 1 lemon half over mussels. Cut remaining 1 lemon half into wedges for serving. Taste broth and season with kosher salt if needed.

Ladle mussels and broth among shallow bowls, then scatter reserved scallions over. Serve with country-style bread or steamed white rice if desired and lemon wedges for squeezing over.

#6595. Popular Thanksgiving Product Recalled From Costco Shelves Over Concerning Contamination Risk

Here's what shoppers need to know ahead of the holiday.

Delish editors handpick every product we feature. We may earn commission from the links on this page.

Costco members, listen up. A popular Thanksgiving topping is being recalled over concerns about possible cleaning chemical contamination. Here's what to watch for.

Costco is recalling its Kirkland Signature Real Heavy Whipped Cream ahead of the upcoming Thanksgiving holiday. The recall covers 15-ounce cans sold between October 11 and October 31, 2026, including those purchased in three-packs.

To identify the affected product, check for item number 1777000, item code AC50, and a best-if-used-by date of April 2, 2027. The cans must also have a printed timestamp between 00:35 and 02:45.

The whipped cream was sold at Costco warehouses in 12 states: Alabama, Florida, Georgia, Iowa, Illinois, Indiana, Missouri, Mississippi, North Carolina, South Carolina, Tennessee, and Wisconsin.

Producer Alamance Foods voluntarily recalled the product after learning that one batch may contain a small amount of a cleaning chemical. According to a November 7 letter sent to Costco members, some shoppers reported a chemical smell and taste.

The company said no serious adverse health effects requiring medical care had been reported. The notice does not identify the chemical or say how it may have gotten into the whipped cream.

If your can matches the affected lot and timestamp, stop using it and return it to your local Costco for a full refund. The company's notice also includes photographs of the can and its printed code to help shoppers identify the product.

For questions or concerns, contact Alamance Foods at customer.care@alamancefood.com.

#6594. There's an Advent Calendar for (Almost) Everything

Souped-up Advent calendars are here to stay this holiday season, with just about every big player in food and beverage getting in on the trend.

Experts say there’s a mix of factors at play as for their rise in popularity: little treats and micro indulgences in an expensive world, the idea of “saving big” on high-value bundles, and the sensory satisfaction of unboxing 25(ish) little boxes leading up to Christmas.

“There’s something so special about having a small treat to look forward to each day,” Sockerbit Scandinavian candy founders Florence Baras and Stefan Ernberg said in a statement. Sockerbit is one of several newbies to the food Advent calendar space this year (and one of our new faves).

Advent Center, a hub for data and reviews for thousands of Advent calendars globally, says there are around 250 food and drink calendars on the market this year. The category makes up about a third of the 2026 calendars it lists.

Max Zeshut, Advent Center’s founder, said food and drink calendars work well because they’re a cheaper, noncommittal entry point into the ritual, compared to, for instance, a beauty box. And for all the new and zany iterations out there, chocolate calendars remain an anchor.

Broadly, the global Advent calendar market is anticipated to grow from $1.32 billion in 2024 to $2.47 billion by 2033, according to research compiled by Accio, a B2B platform. Food and drink calendars hold a huge share of that, with the help of mainstays like Bonne Maman, whose annual calendars have inspired “Jamvent” fan groups for a decade, alongside newcomers that announced inaugural calendars this season.

“As a small team, we try to be very conscious of the operational demands of every product launch,” Fishwife CEO and co-founder Becca Millstein told Bon Appétit. “Still, the demand [for calendars] grew too loud to ignore, so we decided to go for it.”

Millstein cited Fishwife’s success in the online gifting space as motivation to launch a calendar this year. Fishwife’s includes 12 doors of tinned fish and extras, retailing for $150. The company said the calendar’s “elements of surprise and delight” drives chatter and user-generated content on social media.

“In the end, we simply had to do it,” Millstein said.

When the Sichuan condiment company Fly By Jing’s Advent calendar launched in 2024, it sold out in about a month. That’s when founder Jing Gao knew the brand was onto something.

Gao said that 65% of its Advent calendars were purchased by new customers this year and that historically, 20% of customers who purchase a calendar go on to make another Fly By Jing purchase by the end of the year.

“To me, that really speaks to the power of discovery and giving people a chance to explore our flavors in a fun, unexpected way,” Gao said. “We never want that sense of discovery to go away, even for people who have been with us from the beginning. It's become such a fun creative outlet for our team. I think that joy really comes through in the experience.”

The stewards at Onyx Coffee Lab in Arkansas describe a similar phenomenon. “There's so much storytelling, education, and human connection surrounding coffee, and Advent gives us a unique opportunity to explore those things in ways that might not make sense within our everyday offerings,” Onyx’s co-founder Andrea Allen said. Their box features 24 different coffees, each a 56-gram package of whole beans that are roasted on a schedule for peak brewing by their respective reveal day.

At Bonne Maman, Advent calendar planning starts two years in advance. The development team pays close attention to seasonal ingredients and market trends to produce 24 limited-edition jams and spreads made just for the calendar. The result sells out every year, with production growing by 400% since 2017, according to a spokesperson. This year will mark 10 years of the Bonne Maman Advent calendar.

“We’re grateful to the fans who have made it part of their holidays,” a company spokesperson said. “On social media, we see everything from matcha pairings and coffee creations to new takes on toast, along with plenty of flavor-by-flavor reviews. Many fans also write to us to tell us which flavor they loved most. It helps us decide which flavors should return or come in larger sizes.”

Have we stretched Advent calendar hype to its absolute limits? Advent Center’s Zeshut says no.

“The clearest sign of demand is that people search for calendars that don't exist,” he said. “There's no official Monster Energy calendar this year, and 'monster Advent calendar' is still one of the most searched terms that brings people to our site,” he said. “I don't think we've reached peak calendar, but we may have reached peak chocolate.”

#6592. Butternut Pasta With Sausage and Dates

Squash and sausage are a heroic autumnal pairing, especially in a weeknight-friendly pasta. Butternut is the easiest squash to source—not to mention easily found peeled and chopped (a blessing for those with more timid knife skills). But other winter squash like acorn or red kuri can stand in as desired. Whichever squash you select, a sharp, heavy chef’s knife is best for breaking down the chunky veg. But to make your life easier, microwave the squash for 1 to 2 minutes. It will slightly soften, making it simpler—and safer—to slice through.

Rigatoni’s ribbed surface and large holes help chunky squash sauce cling and bites of seared sausage and date wedge—opting for a nutty whole wheat variety will only add to this meal’s autumnal earthiness.

More cozy pastas this way: Balsamic Mushroom and Sausage Pasta; Creamy Red Curry Pasta; and Baked Feta Pasta With Green Sauce.

Cook 1 medium butternut squash (1½–2 lb.), peeled, halved, seeds removed, cut into 1" pieces (about 6 cups), in a large pot of boiling salted water until very tender, 12–14 minutes. Using a slotted spoon, transfer squash to a medium bowl. Reduce heat to low, cover pot, and leave on burner to keep warm.

Heat 2 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil in a large high-sided skillet or a medium Dutch oven over medium-high. Add 1 lb. hot or sweet Italian sausage, casings removed, and break up into small pieces with a wooden spoon. Cook, undisturbed, until deeply browned underneath, about 3 minutes. Continue to cook, stirring occasionally, until browned all over and just cooked through, 3–4 minutes more. Transfer to a plate with a slotted spoon.

Reduce heat to medium-low. Cook 3½ oz. Medjool dates (about 6), pitted, sliced lengthwise ¾" thick, in same pan, turning halfway though, until deeply browned, 3–4 minutes. Transfer to plate with sausage; season with salt.

Add remaining 3 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil to pan. Add 6 garlic cloves, thinly sliced, ½ tsp. freshly ground pepper, ½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt, and reserved squash. Cook, scraping up browned bits and smashing squash with spoon to break up, until lightly browned and broken up into a chunky paste (pieces do not need to be even), about 5 minutes.

Meanwhile, return cooking liquid in reserved pot to a boil over high heat. Cook 12 oz. short tube pasta (such as rigatoni) until very al dente, about 3 minutes less than package directions (it will finish cooking in sauce). Drain, reserving 3 cups pasta cooking liquid.

Add 1 cup pasta cooking liquid to squash and break up squash with spoon until a saucy consistency. Add pasta, another 1 cup pasta cooking liquid, and reserved sausage and dates. Increase heat to medium-high; cook, adding more pasta cooking liquid as needed, until pasta is al dente and coated in sauce, 2–3 minutes. Remove from heat and stir in 1 Tbsp. sherry vinegar or balsamic vinegar. Taste pasta and add more vinegar, salt and/or pepper if needed.

#6591. Phoebe Dynevor Gives a First Look at Her Wedding Ring—and It’s a Timeless Classic

Two months after her marriage to Cameron Fuller, Phoebe Dynevor’s wedding ring has finally been seen out on the town. The actor gave us our first glimpse of the stack on her ring finger while stepping out for coffee in London’s Notting Hill neighborhood—and it proved to be a true classic.

Since her wedding in France this August, Dynevor has worn a simple gold band paired below her gold solitaire oval engagement ring, which features a slender bezel setting. Rather than choosing a style embellished with micro-pavé gemstones or a large eternity ring wrapped with diamonds, the minimal band proves you can let the center stone of your engagement ring do the talking.

Just because the wedding band is simple doesn’t mean Dynevor’s stack is boring, though. Her oval-cut diamond likely sits around three carats, taking up some major real estate on the Bridgerton star’s slender finger. And while the gold band isn’t flashy, the way it pairs with her ring makes it feel modern. Since the diamond on her engagement ring has a low-profile setting, it makes it difficult for another band to sit flush beneath the stone. So rather than tucking underneath the diamond, the band rests at the edge of the stone and leaves some negative space free on Dynevor’s finger. Paired with the engagement ring’s bezel setting—which also offers protection to the diamond—the two rings together lend the stone a floating effect.

Dynevor isn’t the only famous bride who has opted for a simpler gold wedding band as of late. Zendaya and her new husband Tom Holland have each stepped out wearing the minimal ring style since their nuptials, and Anne Hathaway also wears one underneath her large emerald-cut diamond engagement ring. As thicker bands and unique settings have become trendier for engagement rings this past year, we’ve also seen many couples choosing to stick with gold bands to balance out these styles.

The style is a classic for a reason. First, the timeless band remains true to the original symbolism of a wedding ring, whose circular shape represents eternity, unbroken commitment, and mutual fidelity. It’s also an excellent choice for those who lean towards practicality. A simple gold band requires very little maintenance, doesn’t risk losing any stones from improper care, and is easy to wear at all times without needing to remove it. Many people also choose to have gold bands as a spacer ring, which can be worn alongside a more elaborate eternity band given for an anniversary gift or push present down the line.

Engagement and wedding ring trends have changed dramatically in recent years. Lab-grown diamonds are now so popular that many to-be-weds have been looking towards bold styles to stand out, from modern, off-center settings to colorful gemstones and antique jewelry pieces. Phoebe Dynevor’s wedding ring might be a sign that amid the search for originality, you shouldn’t ignore the classics.

#6590. 3 Easy Hacks To Make Instant Mashed Potatoes WAY Better

You might prefer homemade mashed potatoes, but sometimes you just need a shortcut—and on days like that, grabbing the box is WAY easier. But while the back-of-the-box directions will yield just-fine results, a few easy hacks will give you much better results.

As a recipe developer and professional cook, I don’t often make instant mashed potatoes, but I was excited by the challenge of leveling them up—without adding a bunch of extra ingredients or steps that take the convenience out of this convenience food. So I tried making instant mashed potatoes every way I could think of (including the way the box says!). In the end, I found three tricks that, while super simple, massively improve that final bowl of mashed potatoes.

Here are three ways to instantly upgrade instant mashed potatoes.

Most boxes tell you to rehydrate instant mashed potato flakes in hot water enriched with a little butter and a few tablespoons of milk—but I’m going all in on the milk here. The extra dairy really fills out the flavor of the mashed potato and makes it creamier—especially if you’re using a higher-fat milk, like whole or 2%.

When swapping milk for water, it’s best to increase the liquid amount just slightly. For some reason (totally scientific, I’m sure!), the potato flakes require more milk than water to hydrate properly. I recommend 2 extra tablespoons for every half cup of instant mashed potatoes.

Also, add the extra milk the box typically calls for. If you leave it out, the potatoes will be dry. When I was testing, I found it didn’t really matter when that second amount of milk went into the pan (at the beginning versus just before the potatoes), but some boxes emphasize putting it in cold just before adding the potatoes—so if you want to do that to make you feel safer, be my guest!

All the instant mashed potatoes I made lacked seasoning—until I doubled the salt. Then they were perfect. Now here’s the thing: I was testing with Diamond Crystal kosher salt, which is less salty by volume than table salt or Morton’s kosher. The back of the instant mashed potato box didn’t specify what type of salt they used, so if they tested with a fine salt or Morton’s kosher, maybe ¼ teaspoon was the perfect amount. But in my kitchen with Diamond Crystal, it was woefully underseasoned.

Maybe you’re nervous about oversalting and don’t want to double or even slightly increase the salt right away. But regardless, I’m begging you: Taste those potatoes before you serve them and don’t feel bad if you have to add another hefty pinch.

You might assume that mashed potatoes should be made in a pot—I definitely did. But the fluffiest, creamiest instant potatoes I made in this whole testing process came from a wide, high-sided sauté pan. The reason for this? Absolute science.

When adding the instant potato flakes to the hot liquid, the goal is to distribute them as evenly as possible without working them too much. Yes, the back of the box says to “stir” the potatoes in, but in testing, I quickly discovered that even a few strokes can quickly lead to gummy potatoes.

Here’s where the pan size comes in. Using a wide pan increases the liquid's surface area, so you can sprinkle the potatoes evenly over the top and pat them down into the liquid instead of stirring. From there, let them stand until they’ve absorbed the liquid, then give them a few stirs. Trust me: They’ll be way fluffier because you messed with them less!

#6588. 37 Family Dinner Ideas You’ll Make on Repeat

The good news about “family-friendly” dinners? They can be whatever you want them to be. Loaded sweet potato wedges eaten straight from the sheet pan? Absolutely. A dose of nostalgia by way of movie-night sloppy Joes, updated with a fiery kick of gochujang? No question about it. These are dinners for cautious eaters and adventurous ones alike—some familiar, some a little unexpected, and all worth bringing to the table.

Whether tonight calls for a cozy soup (that you can set and forget in your Instant Pot) or easy fish tacos (we have a hunch they’ll become part of your regular weeknight dinner rotation), we’ve got plenty of ideas to keep dinner interesting all year long.

Set tortillas, flaky cod or halibut, spicy lime sauce, and toppings out family-style and let everyone assemble their own piled-high tacos. It’s a simple weeknight family dinner that doubles as a choose-your-own-adventure activity.

Packed with ground chicken, white beans, and canned green chiles, this fast-cooking stew only gets better over time, so make a big batch. We promise, you won’t mind eating it two days in a row.

High-protein cottage cheese replaces often-pricier ricotta in this thrifty-ish spin on a familiar family favorite. More shocking: mozzarella is out too, in favor of tangy super-melter Fontina.

If your family loves pepperoni pizza, they’ll love this baked pasta, which hits all the saucy, spicy, cheesy notes with no takeout required. Roasting the sauce on a sheet pan concentrates its flavor before everything gets a blanket of cheese.

All the appeal of a spicy salmon roll, reassembled as a family-friendly bowl. Pickled cucumber and spicy mayo accompany crackly, broiled salmon cubes for a dinner that’s as fun to eat as it is easy to customize.

Smoky-sweet Korean gochujang lends a hum of heat to this riff on a childhood favorite. Soft buns and a stack of napkins do the rest.

Think chicken pot pie, but in cozy soup form. Complete with crackly, buttery shards of puff pastry you can tear and share, this family meal practically demands a crowd around the table.

This shareable skillet is packed with the flavors of a family-favorite appetizer, with roasted poblanos, red onions, and jalapeños smothered in cheesy sauce.

Store-bought pizza dough makes this family-friendly dinner a snap, even on busy weeknights. This California Pizza Kitchen-inspired recipe is smoky-sweet thanks to barbecue sauce, Gouda cheese, and frizzled mushrooms.

Store-bought zhug, a Yemeni-spiced cilantro sauce, and your broiler are the shortcuts to juicy, charred, baked chicken without a grill. It’s an easy, low-fuss dinner that delivers big flavor.

Somewhere between nachos and loaded potatoes, roasted sweet potatoes get topped with spiced ground beef and briny kimchi for a main dish that’s complete enough to enjoy straight off the sheet pan.

Genuinely juicy, supremely crispy, flavored like falafel, and browned in a skillet for ultimate ease. Serve them with your favorite burger toppings for an easy family dinner.

Sometimes you just want to cook an old faithful—the kind of dinner you know the whole family will love. That’s when you reach for this rich, cheesy, ever-reliable baked ziti.

These vibrant (and vegetarian) kale-and-black-bean-stuffed peppers are a repeat-worthy, one-dish dinner full of hearty flavor. Stirring a dollop of sour cream into the tomato sauce gives it rich texture.

Everyone loves a customizable dinner, and this shawarma-spiced chicken is made for it. Set out warm pitas and all your favorite fixings, like sliced tomatoes and cucumber spears, and let everyone build their perfect plate.

Shrimp cooked in garlicky, lemony butter is bound to be delicious. Serve it with crusty bread or toss it with pasta for a cozy weeknight meal the whole family will love.

Golden-edged tofu meets a bold, spicy satay-inspired peanut sauce in this quick, satisfying dish. Pile it over rice or serve with naan for scooping.

Canned pumpkin is good for way more than sweets. Here, lemon, Parmesan, and chile flakes turn it into a creamy, savory sauce that comes together while the pasta boils.

Spinach-packed dal is a lifesaver on nights when you’re strapped for time but craving something deeply comforting. Serve it with rice or flatbread for a quick vegetarian meal.

Tender soy-glazed chicken meatballs and crisp sesame green beans make a balanced family dinner that needs little else than a pot of rice.

Transform two favorite store-bought ingredients—cheese ravioli and crispy fried onions—into a rich and luscious skillet dinner with a crispy, savory top.

This sunny, dressed-for-summer family dinner relies on a pantry-friendly chicken marinade. All you need: sugar, vinegar, salt, and a few spices. Add couscous and dinner is done.

Make these succulent pork chops when it’s 6:26 p.m. on a Monday and you haven’t figured out what’s for dinner. The sweet-and-savory sauce makes this quick weeknight meal feel planned ahead.

Canned chickpeas and frozen broccoli keep this one-skillet dinner fast and thrifty, while cream cheese delivers on the faux pasta Alfredo front.

Leftover rice meets plenty of fresh ginger, soy sauce, and eggs in this satisfying 20-minute dinner. The key is starting with cold, cooked rice, which crisps up beautifully in a hot skillet.

Cherry tomatoes burst around a block of feta in the oven, forming a tangy, creamy pasta sauce. Calabrian chile paste brings a welcome kick that cuts through the richness.

This hearty catch-all skillet dinner tastes just as good in egg burritos the next morning, or make and freeze it up to three months ahead.

Upgrade grilled salmon with a punchy, vibrant dill chimichurri. It’s quick, fresh, and feels fancy enough to make you feel like you have your life together.

Much faster to make than risotto, this lemony, bright orzotto gets its herby savoriness from a pantry savior: store-bought jarred pesto.

Your favorite party dip, now in pasta form. Frozen spinach and jarred artichokes keep things convenient, while plenty of bubbling cheese makes this skillet dinner every bit as comforting as the original.

So tired you’re considering takeout? Try this simple, speedy stir-fry instead—it comes together in 25 minutes but tastes restaurant-quality.

Store-bought gnocchi bakes up crispy on the outside and pillowy on the inside, the perfect complement to browned spicy sausage and a sprinkle of finely grated Parmesan.

Give mac and cheese the hot wing treatment, because sometimes one comfort food just isn’t enough. It’s creamy, tangy, and just spicy enough to keep you coming back for another forkful.

Let your Instant Pot handle this warm, spicy, protein-packed, family-friendly dinner idea. Top it with a dollop of sour cream, a sprinkle of pickled onions, and whatever else floats your fancy.

Chicken and cabbage may sound pretty basic, but this stir-fry is anything but. Sambal oelek and fish sauce give it plenty of spicy, salty flavor, making it a nutritious family dinner that packs a punch.

Crisp bibb lettuce leaves make the perfect cups for this spicy larb-inspired chicken, which you can dress up with fresh herbs and fried shallots. It’s a fun, hands-on family dinner that gets everyone involved.

This is the kind of salad that can hold its own as a family dinner, packed with roasted sweet potato and tofu, crisp red apple, and a bright, herby green goddess dressing.

#6587. Creamy Miso Mushroom Pasta

Mushroom fans: Bookmark this recipe immediately. It will give you everything you want when you crave a creamy mushroom pasta as soon as the crisp fall air sets in. The hardworking trio of miso, Parmesan, and touch of soy sauce delivers an umami bomb of flavor that doesn’t overwhelm, but magnifies, the best of earthy mushrooms. Coupled with luscious noodles enrobed in a creamy (but not heavy) sauce, what’s not to love?

A few helpful notes for pasta success: (1) While any pasta will work, egg-based noodles, like the fettuccine I recommend here, are the best complement to the sauce. The nests (Rummo and De Cecco are great accessible brands) cook far faster than standard straight pasta, almost as fast as fresh. (2) Don’t be afraid to season your mushrooms! Yes, I know this goes against all that we’ve learned about salting them too early in the cooking process, but just a bit of salt will get them going and releasing their water faster for eventual crisp-browned edges. Don’t be alarmed if you see a pool of water at the start of the mushroom cooking—that’s to be expected and just keep going until it evaporates. (3) Don’t forget to reserve plenty of pasta cooking liquid, which is critical to the eventual sauce’s success. I prefer transferring the al dente noodles from the pasta pot to the skillet, letting any residual water come with it (and to ensure you don’t accidentally drain away that liquid gold).

Find more fall favorite meals here: Weeknight Pumpkin Chili; Cream-ish of Mushroom Soup; Mushrooms au Poivre.

Cook 12 oz. egg-based pasta (such as fettuccine nests) in a large pot of boiling salted water, stirring occasionally, until al dente, about 1 minute less than package directions.

Meanwhile, heat 2 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil in a large skillet over high. Add 1 lb. crimini or mixed mushrooms (such as button, maitake, oyster, and/or shiitake), sliced ¼" thick or torn into bite-size pieces, and ½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt and toss to coat evenly. Spread out into an even layer and cook, undisturbed, until mushrooms are starting to release their liquid, 2–3 minutes (do not be alarmed; there will be a lot). Continue to cook, tossing occasionally, until moisture is almost completely evaporated and edges of mushrooms are starting to brown, 6–8 minutes.

Reduce heat to medium-high; add 5 garlic cloves, thinly sliced, and remaining 1 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil. Cook, tossing often, until garlic is fragrant and golden, 1–2 minutes. Pour in ¾ cup dry white wine, scraping up any browned bits stuck to bottom of pan with a sturdy spatula or flat-edged wooden spoon, and cook until wine is mostly evaporated (you should have about 1 Tbsp. liquid left in pan), about 4 minutes. Reduce heat to medium-low. Add 4 Tbsp. unsalted butter, cut into pieces, and 2 Tbsp. white miso and stir until melted and combined. Slowly pour in ½ cup heavy cream, scraping up any browned bits stuck to bottom of pan; simmer until thickened slightly, 2–3 minutes. Add 1 Tbsp. low-sodium soy sauce; season with freshly ground pepper. Taste and add more salt if needed.

Using tongs, transfer pasta to mushroom mixture and add 1 cup pasta cooking liquid. Increase heat to medium and bring to a simmer. Cook, tossing constantly and adding ½–1 cup more pasta cooking liquid to reach desired sauce consistency if needed, until pasta is al dente and liquid has thickened slightly, about 3 minutes.

Remove pan from heat. Add 1 oz. Parmesan, finely grated (about ½ cup) to pasta and toss to combine. Season generously with more pepper; taste and season with more salt if needed.

Divide pasta among shallow bowls and top with more Parmesan and pepper.

#6586. 85 Gifts You Can Shop on Amazon in 2026 With a Sigh of Relief

Amazon, as you might imagine, has a lot of great gifts. But the Everything Store is simply too vast to wander around hoping the perfect present jumps out at you. And there's plenty worth digging through this year: Amazon and Apple have both rolled out a bevy of new gadgets, it's been a banner year for noise-canceling headphones, and there's some genuinely great clothing to be found among the usual household essentials. Luckily, we've done the rummaging for you, turning up a GQ-endorsed assortment of gifts that look like you put in considerably more effort than a few clicks and two-day shipping.

Still searching? Browse the rest of our gift guides and sign up for the GQ Recommends newsletter for more gift ideas that are actually worth giving.

A teeny-tiny digital camera on a keychain, packaged in a blind box. Half the fun is seeing which retro design you get.

A remote control for turning pages on your Kindle. We have peaked as a society.

Inspired by vintage military watches, Timex's perennial best-selling Expedition Scout has all the rugged charm of a classic field watch, at a price that makes it a no-brainer gift.

The indispensable AirFly gets a touchscreen, taking the guesswork out of pairing your headphones to the seatback screen.

The Kodak Pixpro has emerged as a go-to budget option for anyone looking to embrace the point-and-shoot life.

Timex's classic Ironman Triathlon is a no-nonsense sports ticker with everything you need and nothing you don't.

Other tunes available: “Love Me Tender,” “Fur Elise,” “You've Got a Friend,” “Hey Jude" and so many more.

For the pimple that has the audacity. Everyone needs a little patch sometimes.

Loops' colorfully packaged hydrogel masks make skincare feel more like playtime. An easy bit of self-care for just about anyone on your list.

Tinned fish is an elite stocking stuffer. Especially when it's packaged as beautifully as Fishwife does it.

Momofuku's chili crisp has a way of finding its way onto just about everything, so slip a jar into their stocking and proceed to take credit for every meal they make thereafter.

The iconic Hanes Beefy-T turned 50 this year, and it's still the undisputed heavyweight champion of any dude's T-shirt drawer.

Our pick for the best underwear to buy in bulk, Calvin Klein's stretch briefs are as classic as they get. An easy gift they'll actually use.

The only thing better than a Dickies Eisenhower is a warmer Dickies Eisenhower. This lined version retains everything that makes the original a legend while offering a little extra protection against the cold.

Cashmere is one of life's great pleasures, and Naadam makes it possible to indulge without going broke.

A bomber jacket built to military spec by the brand that made it famous. 'Nuff said, really.

You could get them a fancier hoodie, but there's nothing wrong with sticking to the classics. Russell is an OG in the game, and its Dri-Power fleece hoodie is practically return-proof.

Ralph gave us the gift of the Polo Bear. Now you can give the gift of the Polo Bear on a terrific beanie.

Fact: A guy can always use another polo shirt. Lacoste's iconic cotton-piqué original has the perfect combination of heft and breathability, not to mention nearly a century of good taste behind it.

Time and again, the Levi's 501 ends up right back at the top of our jeans guide. Some things never go out of style, and a great pair of straight-leg jeans is one of them.

Reebok's Club C Vintage has long been a favorite around GQ, and it might just be the best sneaker the Everything Store has to offer.

Browsing, emailing, streaming, the occasional spreadsheet—the Neo handles the everyday stuff without demanding a small fortune for the privilege of owning a fruit-embossed gadget.

Tower 28's travel-size SOS set packs everything they need to stay fresh on the go. A little skincare insurance for wherever the holidays take them.

#6585. I Ate Dinner At 6 p.m. For 30 Days—Here’s How My Body Changed

I have always been someone who eats dinner late. Not intentionally, of course, but between deadlines, meetings, and evening errands, food takes a back seat. The result is a familiar one: I end most days uncomfortably bloated and rarely wake up feeling much lighter.

Tired of feeling this way, I challenged myself to something subtle, for the sake of experimenting: to dinner at 6 p.m. for 30 days, without changing what I ate or restricting calories. Would I wake up less bloated? Would I be ravenous before bed? Would my sleep, digestion, or cravings shift? Before starting, I asked two experts whether the clock matters at all.

Laayla Moon, wellness expert and co-founder of Human Upgrade Fest, is not only encouraging about eating dinner early—she’s practically evangelical. “Eating earlier can make a difference for some people, but it’s not necessarily about the magic of 6 p.m.,” she says. The logic is circadian: our digestive system follows a natural rhythm, much like our sleep cycle, and gut activity slows down at night. A heavy meal close to bedtime can leave you feeling full, but also more uncomfortable and prone to acid reflux; on the other hand, a longer gap between dinner and sleep tends to mean a lighter morning. Moon is candid that evidence for a 6 p.m. dinner (or, simply an earlier dinner time) is still limited. “I believe the real takeaway is to eat in harmony with your body’s rhythm rather than follow a rigid clock,” she says.

Rutu Dhodapkar, a clinical dietitian, agrees. “Evening meal timing should be early for getting digestive comfort, as there should be some time for digestion before sleeping,” she explains. In other words, give your body a head start before you lie down. Her recommended cut-off for busy schedules is more forgiving than mine: “For better results in a busy schedule, it’s advised to have meals early—by 8 p.m. or at minimum, two hours before you go to sleep.”

Both experts were quick to add that timing is only one piece of the puzzle. You could dine at 6 p.m. and still wake up bloated if the meal is enormous, rushed, or washed down with something fizzy. As Moon puts it, “how we eat and what we eat can matter just as much as when we eat—and sometimes, more.”

The “how” piece of this equation starts in the mouth. “Eating slowly and chewing as much as possible also helps for better digestion as enzymes get activated,” says Dhodapkar, while eating quickly, swallowing air and reaching for carbonated drinks are classic routes to gas. The “what,” on the other hand, is very personal: legumes and cruciferous vegetables such as broccoli, cabbage and cauliflower can bother people with sensitive guts, and dairy can be a culprit for those who are lactose intolerant. Moon adds a less obvious factor. “I also think we underestimate the gut-brain connection,” she says, which is a polite way of saying that stress and eating on the go doesn’t help.

Dhodapkar’s advice for anyone attempting a trial like mine was refreshingly low-tech: keep a daily diary. She suggests scoring symptoms from one to ten, noting morning bloating, whether an evening walk eases it, bowel movements, hunger, cravings, and sleep quality, alongside stress, hydration, and your menstrual cycle. This will prevent a good week from being mistaken for a breakthrough.

Initially, this experiment came with intense regret. Hunger, mood swings, and a burning rage of irritability took over my late evenings. I even tried going to bed earlier during the first week to avoid hearing the rumbling noises from my stomach.

But by week two, eating dinner early had slowly, if not entirely, become easier. I no longer felt hungry at night, my late-night bloating had reduced and mornings felt much lighter. An unexpected result of this experiment was my renewed ability to distinguish hunger from boredom.

I ended up eating whatever I craved but noticed that I was less inclined to reach for an additional serving. I had developed a newfound appreciation for early dinners and could finally understand why wellness experts and celebrities alike choose to eat early.

Eating early, it turns out, can help digestion, but it is not a magic fix. Moon is clear that “eating earlier is one useful habit, but it isn’t a standalone solution”. The best routine is one that suits your body, schedule and triggers, which means paying attention to portion size, pace and what actually sits well with you.

One caveat: if bloating is persistent or worsening, comes with severe abdominal pain, blood in the stoo,l or unexplained weight loss, no dinner timetable will fix it. See a doctor. The aim, as Moon says, is not to suppress the symptom but to understand what is causing it.

#6584. Cranberry Pie

What People Are Saying:“I made 3 desserts this Thanksgiving and this was an absolute hit!! Everyone at the table raved about it including my super picky 7 year old who had herself seconds. Definitely a winner and will be making again.” - PurplePuzzle

Preheat your oven to 350° and grease a 9-inch pie plate with butter.

For the crust, grab a large bowl and mix together the Biscoff crumbs, melted butter, and a pinch of salt. Gently press this mixture into the bottom and up the sides of your greased pie plate.

Bake the crust until it turns golden and feels firm to the touch. Once done, set it aside on a wire rack to cool.

In a small bowl, mix the gelatin with some cold water and let it sit so it can bloom.

Next, for the filling, grab a medium saucepan, toss in the cranberries, brown sugar, orange juice, and zest, and bring it to a simmer over medium heat. Stir occasionally while the cranberries burst and the liquid has thickened slightly, which should take about 7 minutes.

Pour in the coconut milk, ginger, heavy cream, almond extract, and a little salt. Stir everything together and heat until it’s nice and steamy, but not quite simmering. Remove from the heat and stir in the bloomed gelatin until fully dissolved.

Now, blend the cranberry mixture until it’s super smooth—use whatever blender or food processor you have handy. Strain it into a bowl, toss out any solids, and let the mixture cool down to room temperature. Pour the cranberry filling into your crust and refrigerate until set, which should take at least 6 hours.

Serve with homemade whipped cream and enjoy!

The full list of ingredients and instructions can be found in the recipe below.

This pie will keep for up to a week in the fridge and frozen for up to 5 months. Simply thaw it out in the fridge the next day and serve.

#6583. Bon Appétit Pick: HelloFresh Ginger Chicken & Rice Bowls

Over the past few years, BA editors have tested just about every meal delivery service out there, and HelloFresh keeps standing out for its bold flavors. So we teamed up with the brand on a 12-week collaboration. The BA Picks collection features recipes hand-selected by our staff, and HelloFresh customers also get an exclusive three-month digital subscription to Bon Appétit. To choose them, we cooked many, many kits in our home kitchens and in the BA Test Kitchen, following the recipe cards exactly. We judged each one on flavor, portion size, cook time, cuisine variety, and the recipe's step-by-step clarity. This Ginger Chicken and Rice Bowl is one of those picks. Here’s what it’s like to make it at home.

As a product tester, I'm very methodical, so I was excited to help build the BA Picks collection. I got to cook a bunch of meals and decide which ones were the best—the same process I take when testing the best pizza ovens or juicers. Despite being Italian, I'm constantly drawn to Asian flavors when I cook at home on weeknights. The balance of salty, sweet, spicy, and acidic is highly addictive. It hits the spot after a long day of reviewing appliances in the Test Kitchen.

That's why the Ginger Chicken & Rice Bowls caught my eye. Made with soy, Thai chili sauce, gochujang, ponzu, and Korean chili flakes, it has all the flavors I crave. It reminded me of some of my favorite BA recipes, like our Gochujang Chicken Stir-Fry, a mainstay in my weeknight rotation. Can a meal kit recipe stand up to a Bon Appétit recipe that's tested over weeks of development? It was my job to find out. (Spoiler alert: It did.)

HelloFresh's Ginger Chicken & Rice Bowls pair saucy ginger chicken with rice, a spicy cucumber side, and toasted peanuts on top. The recipe card rates it easy and lists a total time of 20 minutes. You can order it in two-, three-, four-, or six-serving sizes.

I have an entire container in my fridge dedicated to Asian condiments. If I were cooking this recipe from scratch, I'd have to lug the whole thing out, and the bottles would cover my counter. HelloFresh measures everything out for you, so all you have to do is open the bags and follow the step-by-step instructions.

This kit came with a "mini" cucumber that was more like a normal-size one (perfect for me, since I love cucumber salad). It also had all the seasonings, rice, toppings like peanuts, and chopped chicken breast.

The pre-chopped chicken was the underrated MVP. I rarely cook chicken at home because I hate handling it raw, plus the cleanup that comes after. (Always sanitize your cutting board and prep station after working with raw meat!) So HelloFresh came in clutch here. The only ingredients I had to pull from my own pantry were oil, salt, pepper, and a small dash of sugar.

HelloFresh instructions include photos of each step, so they're easy to follow. I started by putting a pot of rice on. Then I chopped and salted the cucumbers so they could season while I cooked the chicken. After a quick sauté in a pan, I tossed the chicken in the sauce, and it was ready. Once I drained the cucumbers, all I had to do was add the chili flakes, gochujang, sesame oil, ponzu, and sugar. From start to finish, the whole process took me all of 20 minutes. That was great, because the smells coming from each component were making my mouth water.

This dish exceeded my expectations for a meal kit. The cucumbers got a ton of umami from the fermented gochujang dressing, and the chicken was saucy, with a punch of ponzu. The ginger sauce has it all: a sweet, mild ginger flavor, a trace of salty soy, and a hint of heat. Thai chili sauce and ponzu turn it into a sticky glaze for the chicken. The cucumbers add a cooling side and a pop of color, and the peanuts on top are the finishing touch. These are flavors I'd never expect in a delivery box, and I'm super impressed.

Anyone looking to explore Asian ingredients would learn a lot from this dish. It uses gochujang, ponzu, Thai chili sauce, and Korean chili flakes. I'd never cooked with Korean chili flakes (also known as gochugaru), so I was excited to taste it. If you want a quick dinner, this recipe comes together in just 20 minutes. It's a flavorful dish without project-level effort.

The Ginger Chicken & Rice Bowls hit the salty, sweet, spicy, and acidic balance I crave after a long day. The pre-chopped chicken and photo-guided steps make it easy, and there's no counter full of condiments to put away afterward. Find it in the BA Picks collection on HelloFresh, along with an exclusive three-month digital subscription to Bon Appétit.

#6582. Cider-Braised Sausage and Lentils

I haven’t made a meal in the French countryside in fall; but sometimes I dream, and these slow-cooked lentils are what I’d make in such a situation. Back in my American reality, it still makes an excellent dinner or hearty weekend lunch. Look for mild smoked Austrian or German sausages, which lean on mellow herbs and warm spices (sometimes, if you’re lucky, they’re also stuffed with a nutty cheese)—this style is already cooked to a safe temperature, but the casing’s texture is greatly improved when seared before reheating. If your shop only carries sweet Italian sausage or something like an apple-stuffed chicken sausage, both work in a pinch. What a treat it will be to actually finish off that gallon of apple cider you impulsively bought last week in the lentil-braising liquid.

More great fall recipes this way: Charred Cabbage With Sausages and Apples; Pork Chops With Green Chiles and Apples; Mustardy Cider-Braised Pork Chops.

Heat 2 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil in a large high-sided skillet or a medium heavy pot over medium-high. Cook 6–8 smoked Austrian or German sausages (1–1½ lb.), turning often, until deeply browned on all sides, about 4 minutes. Transfer to a plate.

Combine 1 large red or yellow onion, finely chopped, 3 celery stalks, finely chopped, 1 large carrot, peeled, finely chopped, 1 tsp. freshly ground pepper, and ½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt, and remaining 2 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil in same pan. Reduce heat to medium and cook, stirring often and scraping up any browned bits stuck to bottom of pan, until vegetables are softened, 6–8 minutes. Add 5 garlic cloves, thinly sliced, and cook, stirring, just until fragrant, about 1 minute.

Add 2 cups low-sodium chicken or vegetable broth, 1½ cups apple cider, 1½ cups French green lentils, picked through, rinsed, ½ cup finely chopped parsley, 3 Tbsp. Dijon or whole grain mustard, and remaining ½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt to pan. Increase heat to high and bring to a boil. Cook until liquid is slightly reduced, about 5 minutes. Cover pan, reduce heat to medium-low, and cook until lentils are tender and most of the liquid is absorbed but mixture is still saucy, 30–35 minutes.

Uncover pan and stir in 1 Tbsp. apple cider vinegar or red wine vinegar. Nestle sausages into lentil mixture and add any juices pooled on plate. Simmer until sausages are warmed through, about 5 minutes. Top with parsley leaves and reserved celery leaves to serve.

#6581. The Best Veterans Day Food Freebies, From Dunkin’ Donuts To Shake Shack Burgers

A guide to the restaurants thanking veterans with free meals and treats.

Every November 11, Americans celebrate and thank those who have served in our military. Veterans Day marks the anniversary of the 1918 armistice that ended World War I, but it wasn’t until 1954, after both World War II and the Korean War, that it changed nationally from Armistice Day to Veterans Day.

To mark the occasion, many of our favorite national food chains are dishing out free meals, drinks, and treats to both active-duty military and vets. Here’s where you can score big.

Aroma Joe’s is offering veterans free handcrafted coffee or signature AJ’s Rush Energy Drink in any size up to 24 ounces at all locations with a valid ID.

Veterans and active-duty military members can get 10 free Boneless Wings + Fries with valid proof of service at participating BWW sports bars for dine-in only and GO locations with a minimum $5 purchase.

All active military members and veterans can enjoy a free All-American Single Smash or Americana Big Dog in-restaurant.

All active-duty service members and veterans with proof of service can enjoy a free Red, White, and Blueberry Pancake Combo that includes two buttermilk pancakes topped with glazed strawberries, blueberry topping, and whipped topping, along with two eggs, hash browns, and a choice of two strips of hickory-smoked bacon or two pork sausage links.

Active and retired military members can receive a free Original French Toast during operating hours for dine-in orders.

Active-duty, retired military members, and veterans can enjoy a complimentary order of Bang Bang Shrimp and a nonalcoholic beverage when dining at any Bonefish Grill location.

All active and retired military can enjoy a free donut.

All active military and veterans can receive a free single ShackBurger with a valid military ID or proof of service.

All active-duty and retired military members can enjoy a free meal from the chain’s special Veterans Day menu, with the purchase of a beverage when dining in at participating locations. The menu includes the option of 10-Piece Original Wings, Cheeseburger, Buffalo Chicken Sandwich, or Chicken Caesar Salad.

The bagel chain is offering veterans and active military a free coffee and bagel with schmear all day long. The offer includes any size hot or iced coffee and any bagel with any schmear and is only available in the bakery.

Gold Star Families, active military, veterans, and first responders can get a complimentary 5-Course Teppanyaki Entree, including a choice of Hibachi Steak, Chicken, or Salmon. The offer is available for dine-in only and requires the purchase of an appetizer or starter.

Veterans and military members can order a free Spaghetti with Marinara or Meat Sauce with proof of veteran or military status by using the code VET26.

All current and retired military members can enjoy a complimentary buffet and beverage at Golden Corral locations nationwide.

Active-duty military and veterans can enjoy a complimentary choice of 10 Bone-In or Boneless Wings, Beer-Battered Fish & Chips, Steakburger, Chicken Caesar Salad, Buttermilk Crispy Chicken Sandwich, or Chicken BLT Tacos.

Veterans and active military personnel can enjoy a free small hot or iced coffee and a free donut of their choice.

Service members and veterans can receive a complimentary entrée and beverage from a special prix fixe menu, plus a Buy One Get One card, good for a pizza, pasta, or salad with the purchase of one on a return visit between November 12 and 25.

Veterans with a valid military ID can receive a complimentary meal at participating locations when dining in the restaurant between 11 a.m. and 7 p.m.

#6580. The Best New Restaurants in New York City to Visit Now

For some New Yorkers, keeping up with the city’s ever-changing restaurant scene is something of a sport. Indeed, there seems to be a hot new place every week, and sometimes the cadence of openings—as well as rising chefs, new concepts, and freshly renovated rooms—can make your head spin. Of course, there are always the old haunts, the standbys—but isn’t it fun to have some new players on the scene?

There are plenty of fresh restaurants this fall, so if you’re looking for the best and buzziest new restaurants to add to your list, Vogue has you covered. For this list, we focused on places that opened in the past three months. There’s the trio of Bangkok women bringing heartwarming Thai food to a homey West Village space, an Afro-Caribbean brasserie and bakery from an award-winning chef, a beloved South Indian pop-up turned brick-and-mortar gem, and more.

Below, read our picks for the best new restaurants in New York City.

Tucked along the westernmost stretch of Christopher Street, this new Afro-Caribbean bakery and brasserie is making everyone’s mornings a bit cheerier with its sorghum banana bread and beef patty croissants. Calabash opened its doors in early October and is Chef Camari Mick’s first solo restaurant following her role as executive pastry chef of the Musket Room and Raf’s. (She opened alongside chef de cuisine Tajeh Porter.) Daytime service is great for grabbing laminated pastries and breakfast sandwiches from the case, but if you have time to sit down, the fluffy cornbread pancakes drizzled with salted maple sabayon just might ruin all future pancakes for you.

And if you’re really ready to commit (trust me, you are), they’re also offering a five-course prix fixe served Friday and Saturday evenings, with one seating at 6:30 p.m. Dishes like Hoppin’ John Dolma wrapped in collard greens, and red snapper with sweet corn and étouffée-style gravy explore the connections between the diaspora and classical techniques, and are paired with house-fermented mocktails. The restaurant is named for the vessel that has traveled across the African diaspora throughout history, and Chef Mick’s menu highlights traditions found across West Africa, the Caribbean, and America’s Eastern seaboard. As if all of that wasn't worth firing up your OpenTable, I’ve yet to mention the interiors. The 30-seat, 1,300-square-foot space was designed by D.C.-based Drummond Projects (very cozy, very refined), and they also partnered with gallerist Cierra Britton on an exhibition of paintings by BIPOC women artists. —Nicole Kliest, contributing writer

Turn the corner onto East Broadway, past the bustling crowds of Bar Oliver, and you’ll find Cavalier, a Mediterranean-inspired restaurant and wine bar from Chef Mason Lindahl, Tate Jackson, and Yasmin Kaytmaz (who also owns The River). They’ve got pink tables, black leather booths, low lighting, and a private dining room in the back with a dreamlike mural by Georgia Gardner Gray.

The vibe at Cavalier is friendly and earnest, a welcome contrast to the sometimes aloof, cooler-than-thou energy of some of the other nearby see-and-be-seen spots. But the real star here is Chef Lindahl’s food, which feels fancy and comforting all at once. You’ll want to get at least one order of the baked lavash bread, which is served with tomato butter and eggplant, and is so warm and soft you could curl up and take a nap in it.

I also loved the chicken liver mousse, the tender and flavorful duck, and the chocolate mousse for dessert. Double mousse, yes: If it seems decadent, it is, but somehow you leave feeling lighter. They also have what my wine friends call a “serious” wine list, with extensive bottle offerings and fun by-the-glass options, including a red blend from Château Musar, the cult-favorite Lebanese producer. —Anna Grace Lee, lifestyle writer

The vibes might be pleasantly low-key at this new Mexican seafood spot in the West Village, but the food and wine are worth planning an entire evening around. El Camarón Peludo opened this past September on Cornelia Street (next door to the now shuttered Pearl Oyster Bar) and was conceived by the team behind Taqueria Ramirez and Carnitas Ramírez, Giovanni Cervantes and Tania Apolinar, as well as Mexico City-born chef Carlos Barrera. The restaurant is walk-in only, and feels like the love child of a Spanish tapas bar and a quintessential Mexican kitchen.

By their own admission, the menu is an unapologetic celebration of shrimp (all hail the cute crustacean!). Order them raw, chilled, grilled, boiled, or otherwise, and your taste buds are in for a ride. In fact, there’s even a shrimp-shaped lantern hanging above the raw bar, if you appreciate commitment to a theme. Complement all that freshness with their salsa, like the one made from four different chiles, and a wine selection that will knock your socks off. —N.K.

Straker’s is an exercise in controlled chaos. The first New York outpost from Thomas Straker, the TikTok-famous British chef known for his namesake Notting Hill restaurant and “bad boy” reputation, Straker’s is a place where the room is loud, the bouncer wears leather, and the food is excellent.

When I went on a Tuesday a few weeks after opening, the room seemed full of vaguely businessy men and models, everyone’s faces blurring in candlelight, the glow interrupted by the flash of phones eating first. Is this the place to come for a long overdue catch-up with a friend, or a first date? No. I want to come here with three friends and sit in the corner sipping martinis while the loud, untz-untz music bass-shakes the banquettes and drowns out our gossip.

I could easily eat two of the wood-fired mussel flatbread, which is like pizza crust dipped in buttery mussel sauce. The duck was tender, the potatoes perfectly crispy. Dessert is also important. The rainbow array of ice creams is sure to spark debate (we went with the burnt honey, which was nice and not too sweet), but no matter what you do, get the chocolate tart. Don’t skip the cucumber salad either, which offered a pleasingly fresh crunch to balance out the indulgence—though indulgence is the name of the game here. That is, of course, if you can get a reservation. —A.G.L.

Adding to the city’s dynamic supper club scene, chef Lana Lagomarsini opened Creola on the Upper East Side this past September, following her time as chef de cuisine at Francis Mallmann’s Garzón in Uruguay, as well as cooking stints at Gramercy Tavern, Daniel, and Momofuku Ko. The opening menu kicked off with flavors like elk with blackberry jerk and plantain, and an oxtail pâté en croûte (evoking a Jamaican beef patty). The wines are sourced from low-intervention producers from France and Spain, and can either be paired with each course or purchased by the glass or bottle. (Top points for the fact that every bottle is priced under $100!) Fortify your appetite for dessert, which at the moment is a sassafras flan crowned with a poached cherry and bay leaf oil.

The restaurant’s name is a sentimental homage to Lagomarsini’s grandmother, Creola, who lived on the Upper West Side and crossed Central Park every afternoon to pick her up from school, located just five blocks from where the restaurant now stands. There’s even a framed photo of her grandmother that hangs in the dining room, which makes the experience feel all the more intimate and homey. Speaking of the interiors, the design was impressively handled by Lagomarsini herself, who sourced antique furniture and hemmed the curtains by hand. Creola has 12 seats and is open Wednesday through Saturday beginning at 5 p.m. with two seatings a night. —N.K.

When I heard that the Portuguese chef Nuno Sousa—of Leitão in the West Village, where I’ve enjoyed tapas and not-too-sweet margaritas—was opening a new restaurant nearby on West 10th Street, I was curious to try it. Galo, which is in a historic 1860s carriage house, is a warm space decorated with ceramic art where you can have suckling pig, octopus that slices as smooth as butter, and tender picanha. They have an extensive Portuguese wine list, but I loved the Só mais uma cocktail (a refreshing mojito-like mix of gin, matcha, mint, lime, and Portuguese herbal liqueur), and the potato pavé, which was crispy and crunchy like thin slices of potato paper. —A.G.L.

Hommali is the debut restaurant from a team of three Thai women—chef Chattchakorn “Benz” Khajornchaisan, general manager Kritayanee “Air” Promsarin and operations lead Pichalak “Picha” Srigungvarl—all Bangkok natives who became friends while working in the New York City restaurant scene. They’ve put a lot of hometown heart into Hommali, which takes its name from hom mali, which is Thai for “fragrant jasmine rice.”

You can feel the camaraderie in the air of the cozy West Village space. Paintings from Bangkok’s Chatuchak Weekend Market line the walls of the den-like downstairs dining room, and dishes like tom yum seafood cocktail are served in a beautiful shell. I loved the Panang curry beef cheek and the five-spice duck with duck fat rice, plus the passionfruit cocktail with a bubble-bath-like topping, and delicious toasted rice ice cream with coconut for dessert. —A.G.L.

Over the past few years, Top Chef alum Rasika Venkatesa has built up a devoted following with her Mythily pop-ups. Now, Chef Venkatesa’s progressive South Indian restaurant has found a brick-and-mortar home in Williamsburg. Named in honor of Venkatesa’s grandmother, the restaurant draws on her childhood in Chennai, techniques she learned while traveling across Tamil Nadu, and her fine-dining training at The French Laundry and Mourad.

When I went for dinner not long after its opening in late September, every table was full. People craned their necks to look at the vibrant, artful dishes landing on each table. I got my spoon out to scoop up all the delicious, creamy sauce of the Lamb Sukka Dumplings, which is a must-order, along with the Benne Dosa, the chicken, and the confit potato roast with sambar béarnaise, plus the “filter coffee soft-serve.” —A.G.L.

Some of my most memorable meals have been in Brazil (first time ant consumption, for example), and while I don’t have immediate travel plans to return to the South American culinary capital, thankfully, I have Iara. Chef Vitor Mendes’s new restaurant in the Lower East Side takes inspiration from the Amazon Rainforest and is named for the region’s water goddess. The 60-seat, open-kitchen concept was designed by New York-based practice Studio WDM and channels the Amazon’s soil for its painterly color palette (swirls of chocolate brown, burnt oranges, and terracotta dance across the walls and tables).

Menu-wise, it’s basically a who’s who of Amazonian heavyweight flavors: tapioca crisps gilded with smoked trout mousse and biquinho pepper, cheese bread with smoked eggplant dip, Brazilian red snapper stew with red palm dendê oil, tucupi, and coconut milk. If you’re looking to impress your dining mate, go for the charcoal-grilled tambaqui, a large Amazonian river fish that the team brushes with a spice blend and serves alongside stewed butter beans, tapioca fries, and açaí ketchup. —N.K.

These days, the word “sexy” is thrown around a lot when describing a restaurant, but 148 Noble actually is sexy. The French and New Orleans-inspired bistro, on a quiet residential street in Greenpoint, is candlelit and cozy. It’s small, but not too small. The service is attentive, with a slightly conspiratorial air that makes you feel like you’re all in on the same secret. A misstep is corrected by a heavier-than-usual wine pour. Yes, the portions might be a bit small, but every bite is flavorful. The chef, Gabriel Borges, is from New Orleans and used to work at Chez Ma Tante down the street. Bring your date and get the pommes paillasson (a Jenga tower of fancy French fries, basically), the duck with honeynut squash and pickled ají dulce, and the rich chocolate tarte with crème fraîche. —A.G.L.

Why have a normal-portioned meal when an all-you-can-eat buffet is an option? It’s a fair question to ask yourself prior to arriving at Good Time Country Buffet, which translates a cherished Southern dining tradition to the East Village. This is the third restaurant from Good Time Hospitality, the same team behind Kisa and C as in Charlie. If you’ve been to either of the aforementioned hotspots, you’re already aware the team was born in Korea and raised in Atlanta, with both of these distinct culinary identities cleverly finding their way onto the menus.

For this concept, they turned to the classic buffets they grew up going to, and programmed the menu to be a fixed-price, self-serve extravaganza. Fried chicken, collard greens, cornbread, mac and cheese, ice cream sundaes—the sky’s the limit, friends. And as far as inspiration goes, they didn’t stop at the menus. The interiors were designed by Two Point Zero and echo classic country buffets with wood paneling, patterned wallpapers, and—rather thoughtfully—carpeted floors, which traditionally have been used to ensure seniors don’t slip and fall while getting their buffet on. (Seniors coming to Good Time Country Buffet also receive a discounted price.) This opening especially strikes a chord with co-owner David Yun, who, as a kid, joined produce delivery routes to Georgia country buffets with his father, who still works in the same role. As part of the restaurant’s research and development process, Yun rejoined his father on those routes. —N.K.

Humm, Daniel Humm’s first namesake restaurant, is about as buzzy as it gets. The cavernous 7,731-square-foot space—which was home to EN Japanese Brasserie for 20 years—has been transformed by Humm and interior designer Pierre Yovanovitch, along with artists Francesco Clemente and Rashid Johnson. The room glows with light from taper candles encased in glass on each table. A sunset tile mural frames the 16-foot wood-fired hearth oven, and it all feels a little like being in another world for the night. Everyone gets the caviar bagel, which is good (it’s a miniature bagel with caviar, after all), but my favorite dishes were the tomato focaccia and the milk and honey soft-serve sundae. —A.G.L.

In a sea of nostalgic-themed restaurants, Booth’s Extra Fine should go to the top of your must-try list. It’s not a club masquerading as a steakhouse; it’s the real deal. Chef Nick Pfannerstill, who worked at the now-closed Michelin-starred restaurant Dovetail and is co-owner of the cocktail bar Nobody Told Me, is serving smoky steaks that cast a pleasant aroma over the room, cold and balanced martinis, a butter roll that glistens, Caesar salad with garlic bread-like croutons, shrimp voodoo. Everything I had was delicious, and it was fun to try various sauces on offer, including salsa verde and aged brandy peppercorn. For dessert, get the bourbon chocolate cake, which may fulfill my years-long search for a chocolate cake as decadent as the one in Matilda. —A.G.L.

#6579. Ayo Edebiri Got the Forehead Curl Memo

Ayo Edebiri is one of the best-dressed people in Hollywood. In 2024, GQ named her a rising star in menswear. At our 2026 Men of the Year party, she made an even stronger case for herself as a style icon for the ages. Walking the red carpet at the Chateau Marmont in West Hollywood, the Emmy-winning actor continued her winning streak of power suiting in a navy chalk-stripe ensemble, a bright emerald-turquoise dress shirt, and a burgundy geometric tie. Her bob was styled in a side part, with a pronounced curl sweeping across her forehead. It’s a look that’s become a staple among Hollywood’s best-dressed men this year, a callback to Superman’s signature swoop, minus the Spandex tights and cape.

In the 1920s, the playful wisp of hair was known as the kiss curl: a deliberately placed lock of hair that sat on the forehead, even amid an otherwise carefully sculpted ’do. (As Seth Rogen helpfully pointed out on Instagram after we noted the kiss curl’s 2026 resurgence: “It’s called a Forelock.”) Its prominence in men’s grooming can be traced back in part to the French-American entertainer Josephine Baker, whose iconic curl ushered in an era—and now a century—of rogue forehead curls.

The kiss curl was so emblematic of the era that it made a triumphant return at the 2025 Met Gala, themed “Superfine: Tailoring Black Style.” A host of women paired the look with impeccable tailoring, including Simone Biles, Taraji P. Henson, Teyana Taylor, and, yes, Ayo Edebiri.

The modern appeal of the forehead curl is easy to understand. As hairstyles have grown longer, looser, and less structured, the curl lends an air of studied nonchalance—as if you didn’t spend too much time getting your hair just right. It’s sexy in a just-got-out-of-bed kind of way, especially when everything else—from the rest of the hair to the outfit—remains crisp, clean, and pristine.

As Edebiri once told Vogue of dressing for the red carpet: “One of the fun parts of getting to do this sort of thing is that you get to transform and be these different permutations of yourself.” At GQ’s Men of the Year party, she once again understood the assignment.
