#6578. The USDA Thinks I Can Live on $65 a Week. Can I?

Welcome to The Receipt, a series documenting how Bon Appétit readers eat and what they spend doing it. Each food diary follows one reader’s week of expenses related to groceries, restaurant meals, coffee runs, and every bite in between. In this time of rising food costs, The Receipt reveals how folks—from different cities, with different incomes, on different schedules—are figuring out their food budgets.

In today’s special edition of The Receipt, we're unmasking the diarist and following James Beard Award-winning writer Paul Greenberg—a self-described cheapskate—on his quest to live on the USDA's Thrifty Food Plan.

My friends sometimes mistake me for a survivor of the Great Depression and not a Gen X-er raised in a household free from deprivation. I don't just bargain hunt. I bargain scour as if it were 1931.

This habit stays with me no matter if I’ve got a book on the bestseller list or if the stock market has just tanked. As a lifelong fisherman, I love angling for opportunities lolling in the currents of American commerce. I can’t stand the idea of buying a $5 gallon of milk when I know that the same milk from the same cows is lurking at a supermarket across the street for under three bucks.

With the inflationary surge of recent years, my friends have at last started to take a curiosity in the methods of my madness. According to the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, the price of sirloin steak is up 21% since January 2024. Romaine lettuce? 27%. Even a gosh darn cup of coffee will cost you over 50% more in 2026 than it did when the Kansas City Chiefs last won the Superbowl. So when Bon Appétit asked my cheapskate self if I could get through a week of groceries for below what the USDA stipulates as its “thrifty food plan,” I smiled the knowing smile of an old-timer. Bon Appétit and USDA, I accept your challenge.

The USDA established the Thrifty Food Plan in 1975 and updated it in 2021 in an attempt to model a healthy diet that hits all the food groups. The TFP, as we’ll call it here forward (to economize on words in these lean times), proposes different shopping lists for different genders and age groups. I took those 2021 numbers and adjusted them for 2026 inflation. As a man in his 50s, I was given a total allotment of $64.90 per week, and recently, I took to the weird yet familiar corners all over New York City at which I procure my groceries. Using my usual regular shopping list, I mostly beat those numbers across the board—without, as US Agriculture Secretary Brooke Rollins recently suggested, resorting to a nutritionally suspect “$3 a meal for a piece of chicken, a piece of broccoli, you know, a corn tortilla and one other thing.”

However, the experiment raised a deeper question: Should I have to? But first, here’s how I did it.

Out of habit or laziness, many of us have a “favorite grocery store.” In an era of rapacious capitalism that has pushed so many Americans toward insolvency, there can be no favorites. Rather, it pays to seek out places where merciless competition drives major chains towards a common bargain basement. In Manhattan, where I live, I call these places “golden corners”—spots where Trader Joe’s, Target, and the rising star of discount grocery chains, Lidl, cluster together around a single intersection.

I’m able to easily deduce which place offers the lowest prices and run between them in a single shopping outing. While I’ll occasionally venture elsewhere for my meat and dairy (see: Chinatowns, featured later in this article), I find a good cutthroat corner serves me best when looking for animal protein.

Note: There is no beef on this list. For climate change reasons, I’ve never been a fan of the world’s most carbon-intensive protein, and to my mind, the three-dollars-cheaper-per-pound ground turkey works just fine in a Bolognese. Also note that neither the TFP nor I put any cheese on our lists either. I’m not sure why TFP refrained, but after beef, cheese is one of the most climate impactful animal proteins on the planet. The environmentalist in me also says cut the cheese.

Professional economizers often encourage us to choose vegetables and fruits with longer shelf lives that can bang around in our fridges until we’re ready to eat them. I’ve found picking the cheapest fruits and vegetables when they’re available is ultimately a better deal. For this, I turn to a staple of American urban street life: the fruit cart.

Fruit cart vendors, common in New York, Los Angeles, Miami, and Chicago, buy produce wholesale and offer deep discounts, especially when shelf life is short. My go-to cart-guy in Lower Manhattan nearly always has a $1 special (cauliflower, cucumbers, asparagus, berries of all kinds) and the relationship we’ve built means he steers me toward what’s good.

What if the nearly overripe berries go off? To this I say: There is no berry too off that can’t be made into jam (which saves you in the miscellaneous category at this article’s end). As for salad greens, while the mainstream shopping world wrings its hands over cyclosporiasis, I’ve found that joining a community garden circumvents the dreaded disease while also purging the scourge of inflation from your wallet. My community garden costs me about $50 a year in membership fees, seeds, and fertilizer, plus about an hour of my time a week in tending. The buy-in amounts to roughly $0.50 per salad.

Whatever fruit carts and my garden can’t supply, I usually find at great prices in Manhattan’s Chinatown, likely because vendors have connections to a handful of small farms and wholesalers that operate outside of most mainstream supermarkets. According to the California Migration Museum, there are roughly 50 Chinatowns across America in nearly every major American city, which is to say that a lot of the country should have access to one.

Note: Even with bargain basement shopping, I only barely hit USDA’s fruit mark. This was because nearly half of USDA’s fruit budget is juice, which, to my mind, is a bit like calling ketchup a vegetable.

The TFP drives a hard bargain on grains, expecting the home shopper to plunk down $3.76 for an entire week’s worth of “refined-grain staple grains," which include rice, pasta, bread, tortillas and the like. That’s tough when a loaf of Wonder Bread at Walmart costs you $2.47. Add a single box of one-pound pasta and it could send you over-budget.

There’s a bit more give in the "whole-grain staple grains" category, which allows $6.94. But even a whole-wheat loaf from Walmart (priced at $2.97) eats up just over half of my weekly allotment.

The only way I was able to snag the bread, rice, and pasta in my weekly shop and stay under budget was by leaning on another Asian country and by working hard on my home turf.

Patel Brothers, a national chain of Indian grocery stores, sells brown and white rice as well as beans of all flavors and provenances for prices that range from $0.80 to $2 per pound. As for bread, Target’s house brand of whole wheat flour is $2.69 for a five-pound bag. About a pound and a quarter of it makes a loaf. Weekly sandwich bread therefore costs out at $0.67 per loaf.

Last and actually also least: pasta. Nobody but nobody beats Trader Joe’s buck a pound.

Shopper beware—the last-minute, forgotten miscellaneous item is often the thing that stings you most at the register. Salt, sugar, cooking oil, and coffee purchased last minute, at even a cheap store, can be double what you’d pay if you are keeping careful track of who's charging what at your local golden corner. Keeping a passive list in your head of where the best buys on miscellany live helps these kinds of rookie mistakes from happening.

Additionally, as above, a little home elbow grease can be surprisingly effective in the condiment aisle. Fruit cart fruit made into jam and an immersion-blended home mayonnaise (a commitment of two minutes max) cost you pennies. And then there’s online. I have yet to find a better deal on coffee than on Amazon.

So I did it. I filled my fridge, stocked one shelf of my pantry, and even had a little left to treat myself to breakfast after this exhausting pan-city forage. Here’s what the final numbers looked like:

Does this mean the USDA’s stingy allowance is appropriate for these ever more expensive times? That anyone can be a successful cost-cutter like me?

Um, no. My kids are grown. I’m a freelance writer with weird hours. I live in a vast, quirky city with odd corners that can cost out cheaper than parts of the developing world. A busy working mom in a food desert who can’t commit to a community garden would find the ordeal a heavy lift.

Thank you for joining me on this ride through my own personal Great Depression. But as for you, USDA, I think it’s time you upped your budget. Stop cutting things like food stamps and healthcare. Perhaps the newest iteration of Congress will be more inclined to make this happen than its predecessor. We are, after all, among the wealthiest sovereign nations in the world.

C’mon, America! Don’t be such a cheapskate.

#6577. Broiled Salmon Teriyaki

Sometimes all it takes to make dinner feel special is a big, bold piece of protein. Case in point: This salty-sweet salmon glazed in a glossy teriyaki-style sauce. Brushed in two rounds with the quick sauce made with nothing more than sugar, soy sauce, sesame oil, and vinegar, the salmon sizzles under the broiler, charring as it takes on a smoky flavor. This recipe calls for one large piece of salmon, but you can use smaller fillets or opt for a white fish such as cod or halibut. Just note that the cooking time will be shorter if using smaller pieces, so keep an eye on them. Add a quick garnish of sliced scallions and toasted sesame seeds, and dinner is done.

More salmon winners this way: Hot Honey-Glazed Salmon; Green Curry-Glazed Salmon; and Slow-Roasted Salmon With Harissa.

Bring ⅓ cup (packed; 67 g) dark brown sugar, ¼ cup soy sauce, 2 Tbsp. unseasoned rice vinegar, and 2 tsp. toasted sesame oil to a simmer in a small saucepan over medium-high heat; cook until reduced by half and syrupy, 5–7 minutes. Let sauce cool until thickened slightly, about 10 minutes.

Heat broiler (if broiler is in your oven, place rack in upper third). Season both sides of one 1½–2-lb. skinless or skin-on center-cut salmon fillet with kosher salt. Place, skin side down, in a skillet or baking dish. Transfer one third of sauce to a small bowl and set aside for serving. Brush about half of remaining sauce over fillet. (If the salmon has a lot of room around it in the pan, line with foil to prevent runoff sauce from burning onto pan.)

Broil salmon until sauce is just starting to burn in spots, 4–7 minutes. Brush remaining sauce over fillet and broil until deeply charred and salmon is opaque all the way through, about 5 minutes.

Remove fish from oven and spoon reserved sauce over. Top with thinly sliced scallions and/or toasted sesame seeds if desired.

#6574. Andrew Garfield’s Hair Is the Mane Attraction

Andrew Garfield’s hair is very long—and oh so glorious. When the 43-year-old actor sat down with GQ for his 2026 Men of the Year interview, he told us he’d grown his current shoulder-length mane for his role as Roy Horn (of Siegfried & Roy tiger-wrangling fame) in the upcoming series Wild Things. Production ultimately put him in a wig, but Garfield kept the length regardless. And thank goodness he did. The actor brought his enviable mane to the red carpet at our annual Men of the Year party at the Chateau Marmont in Los Angeles on Thursday night, where it held its own among Hollywood’s finest.

The Artificial star arrived in an Edward Sexton suit, accessorized with a Breguet watch. But, as has been the case lately, his hair was the real headliner. The neck-grazing length was in fine form, with a few stray strands tucked neatly behind his ears. And then there was the forehead curl: a particularly on-trend flourish that’s found its place atop some of this year’s best-dressed stars (including Ayo Edebiri).

We first caught a glimpse of Garfield’s longer locks at Wimbledon this summer in London. At the time, his longtime hairstylist, Lucy Halperin, let us in on the secret to the look: a little sea salt spray, styling cream, and a diffuser to bring out his natural curls and waves. The combination enhances the hair’s volume while keeping frizz at bay.

That said, Halperin also credits his good hair to a bit of genetic luck. “Sometimes we just give it a good little wet down, and it kind of just works with him,” she told us at the time.

Whatever transformations Garfield has in store for his next on-screen role, we hope this particular look sticks around. Because if Thursday night was any indication, he’s not quite ready to part with it—and frankly, neither are we.

#6572. Chili Crisp Yogurt Chicken

Slather Greek yogurt and your favorite chili crisp on chicken thighs, roast in a hot oven, and you’ll be rewarded with juicy, tender meat with a delightful orange-tinged exterior. But the best part of this sheet-pan dinner comes after the chicken is cooked: Spread cooked rice into the pan’s juices, then slide the baking sheet back into the oven. As the rice soaks up the deeply savory sauce, it will crisp in spots, creating a texture that’s somewhere between chewy-fluffy steamed grains and a freshly toasted pita chip. And when it comes to chili crisp, we love the iconic and easy-to-source Lao Gan Ma, but specialty brands like Fly By Jing are great too—just make sure the one you use is not too spicy, which will overpower the dish.

More great chicken and rice recipes this way: One-Pot Chicken Thighs With Cilantro Rice and Beans; Spiced Coconut Chicken Rice; Nana’s Chicken and Rice Stew.

Preheat oven to 425°. Season 6–8 skinless, boneless chicken thighs (1½–2 lb.) with 1 tsp. Diamond Crystal or ½ tsp. Morton kosher salt.

Whisk together ¾ cup plain whole-milk Greek yogurt and ¼ cup plus 2 Tbsp. well-stirred chili crisp in a large bowl. Add chicken thighs and toss to coat.

Arrange chicken on a rimmed baking sheet and top with any yogurt mixture left in bowl. Bake chicken until deeply browned and an instant-read thermometer inserted into the thickest part of a thigh registers 165°, 25–30 minutes. Transfer chicken to a cutting board or plate.

Spread 3 cups cooked jasmine or short-grain rice over baking sheet with chicken juices and bake until most of the juices have been absorbed and rice is starting to crisp in spots, 12–15 minutes.

Meanwhile, whisk together 1 Tbsp. finely grated lime zest, ¼ cup fresh lime juice, ½ tsp. sugar, ¼ tsp. Diamond Crystal or Morton kosher salt, and remaining ¼ cup plain whole-milk Greek yogurt in a small bowl.

Combine ½ medium head of green cabbage (about 1 lb.), very thinly sliced, and a big pinch of Diamond Crystal or Morton kosher salt in a large bowl. Using your hands, scrunch cabbage gently to soften. Add 1 small red onion, thinly sliced, 1 cup finely chopped cilantro, and yogurt dressing and toss to combine. Taste cabbage slaw and season with more salt if needed.

Slice chicken as desired and serve with crisped rice and cabbage slaw.

#6570. Seeing Green on the GQ Men of the Year Red Carpet

The carpet at our annual GQ Men of the Year party may be red, but we’re seeing—dare we say it—Brat green.

Last night, as the stars of our latest MOTY issue gathered at the iconic Chateau Marmont, we noticed a verdant trend emerge on the carpet. Who better to kick things off than two of the most boisterous creatives from our 2026 Breakout Stars crew? First up was actor-comedian Stavros Halkias, who sported a screaming lime green suit by Alan David, a matching Cego silk shirt, and olive-hued Bottega Veneta loafers. Not far behind was Club Kid director-star Jordan Firstman, who also greened out in a full runway look from Anthony Vaccarello’s final menswear collection for Saint Laurent: a boxy, greenish khaki suit with bejeweled buttons, layered over a liquid-silk chartreuse shirt. Both ensembles sure were bright, but ask any color theorist and they’ll probably tell you that wearing green on a red carpet is a surefire way to stand out—they’re opposite of each other on the color wheel for a reason!

The chartreuse looks just kept on coming: the one and only Ice Spice donned a flowing green DSquared2 dress, with matching green eyeshadow (and a curiously hirsute handbag) to boot.

Elsewhere on the carpet, The Bear’s Ayo Edebiri—already a bonafide menswear star—opted for a different but equally striking shade of green. Her sleek striped power suit by London-based designer Connor Ives popped thanks to a kelly green shirt and a contrasting crimson tie. (Edebiri wasn’t the only woman who rocked tailoring on the MOTY carpet this year: model Cara Delevingne, who stars in Firstman’s Club Kid, wore a slouchy-chic black suit by Saint Laurent, while Luciana Damon, wife of cover star Matt, layered a tuxedo-style bolero jacket over her gown.)

If the MOTY red carpet can provide any insights into the year of fashion ahead, we’ll surely be seeing even more green in the months to come. We’re manifesting abundance, in more ways than one.

#6569. Soothing Rice Porridge

This is a Japanese-style rice porridge known as okayu. I ate this every morning in the early weeks of postpartum after my first daughter was born. It’s what our family reaches for whenever we need a simple, nourishing dish that warms from the inside out. For the smoothest porridge, let the rice soak in cold water before cooking.

If you have time, soak the rice, which makes the texture softer and can aid in digestion. Place washed rice in a bowl and pour in water to cover by 1". Soak at least 30 minutes and up to 4 hours. Drain off excess water before starting the recipe. The wakame seaweed, which you’ve probably had in miso soup, can typically be found dried anywhere Asian groceries are available.

In The Fourth Trimester, we ask parents: What meal nourished you after welcoming your baby? This month it’s a cozy rice porridge by Eating at Home cookbook author Trinity Mouzon Wofford. Read more: Breakfast at Home, After Birth at Home.

Combine 1 cup short-grain rice, washed, soaked if desired, ¼ cup dried wakame (seaweed), 1 Tbsp. dried red shiso, and 6 cups low-sodium broth (any kind) or water in a large donabe, medium Dutch oven, or other heavy pot. Cover and bring to a boil over medium-high heat (you’ll hear bubbling). Uncover and stir, making sure nothing is stuck to bottom of pot. Cover and reduce heat to low. Continue to cook porridge 30 minutes more (resist the urge to peek).

Remove pot from heat and let porridge sit (still covered) 10 minutes. Uncover and stir. Rice grains should be cooked through, broken open, and creamy, but porridge should still be fairly loose. Season porridge with fine sea salt.

Ladle porridge into bowls and serve, topped with toasted sesame seeds, toasted sesame oil, and/or thinly sliced scallions.

#6568. In Puerto Rico, It's Not Thanksgiving—It's Sanguiving

Puerto Rican Thanksgiving is an exhilarating holiday remix. Think turkey marinated in garlic, lime, and oregano, then stuffed with fried green plantains and chicharrón mofongo. Gravy is more likely to be made with guava than with giblets, and flan stands in for apple pie. “Pumpkin spice” is nowhere to be found; here, the local winter squash calabaza takes center stage. And in lieu of warm apple cider, sweet coconut water is sipped beachside straight from a coco.

Thanksgiving is just as cherished in Puerto Rico as it is on the mainland. Celebrated locally since the early 20th century, shortly after the United States invaded in 1898, it marks the beginning of the island’s rambunctious holiday season. It is also a favorite of chef and restaurateur Giovanna Huyke, who over four decades has become the feast’s culinary authority in Puerto Rico.

I meet with Huyke, widely considered the Puerto Rican answer to Julia Child, on a hot summer day at SatoFino, a neon-hued, woman-owned restaurant in San Juan. The bartender quickly spies her—Huyke is a regular, and her signature red hair makes her easy to spot—and prepares the chef ’s go-to drink, a stiff Manhattan. We settle into our barstools, readying to plan what will ultimately unfurl into an epic cooking adventure. Huyke has a propensity for them, she tells me. In the preceding days she traveled to Atlanta to cook for Ser Familia—a nonprofit that specializes in supporting Hispanic families—before she rushed back to Caguas, a city 20 miles south of San Juan, where she fed VIPs attending the Miss Universe Puerto Rico pageant. Then she raced across the island to teach a traditional-methods cooking class in San Germán, the second-oldest city in Puerto Rico. Now, she’ll show me how to prepare a Puerto Rican Thanksgiving feast.

A vueltita through the Plaza del Mercado de Río Piedras with a fresh haul of groceries, in preparation for Sanguiving.

“We have a rich and resilient food history—it came from necessity, lack, and a bounty from the land,” Huyke says. It’s a complex cuisine informed by both a deep agricultural heritage and a modern reliance on imported and shelf-stable ingredients, which, despite many obstacles, manages to emerge beautiful and full of flavor—the continuation of a culinary evolution ongoing for centuries. “Our food comes from Spain, Indigenous Taíno people, and [enslaved] West Africans,” Huyke continues. “But it grew from our land and from our history, mixing every influence in our pilónes and our cauldrons.”

Being around Huyke is a joy. A local TV personality, newspaper columnist, and cookbook writer since the late ’80s, Huyke has taught generations of Puerto Rican home cooks how to prepare the island’s most treasured dishes. Among them was my grandmother, Sara, who I call Tata. Like many members of the Puerto Rican diaspora, my family traveled back to the island for the festivities, alternating each year between Thanksgiving and Christmas. We’d enter Hartsfield- Jackson International Airport in Atlanta in heavy winter coats and leave San Juan’s Luis Muños Marín in shorts and tank tops.

Tata’s Thanksgiving table centered on the expected turkey, but her stuffing was exceedingly Puerto Rican. To a base of Pepperidge Farm stuffing mix, she added picadillo: ground beef cooked with sofrito—the fragrant blend of garlic, onions, peppers, and the punchy native herb culantro that is the cornerstone of the Puerto Rican palate—and pimiento-stuffed Manzanilla olives, all seasoned with the golden spice blend sazón. When Tata died I inherited a weathered copy of Huyke’s 2004 recipe booklet Celebraciones. Within it were recipes that clearly informed Tata’s tremendous Thanksgiving menu; it turned out Huyke had been influencing my holiday for even longer than I knew.

Although formally known in Puerto Rico as El Día de Acción de Gracias, in true Boricua fashion, Thanksgiving is often referred to as Sanguiving, a play on words that gestures to the Roman Catholicism that remains the region’s predominant religion. It’s also El Día del Pavo, which directly translates to “Turkey Day,” and Sangiving, spelled like it sounds. We islanders have a fondness for clever, shortened expressions, an example of our natural tendency toward Puertorriqueñizar—in English, “to make Puerto Rican.”

A stall brims with large slabs of local calabaza.

“Our adobo goes on the turkey, and all the sides have something to do with sofrito,” Huyke tells me, walking me through the standard Puerto Rican Thanksgiving table. In Puerto Rico, adobo takes two forms—one wet and one dry. Each is a spectacular blend of Spanish, African, and Indigenous ingredients and techniques—garlic, onion, peppers, and herbs pounded in a wooden mortar and pestle with Taíno roots called a pilón, binding the island’s ancestral and colonial cultures.

Puerto Ricans officially became American citizens (and draft eligible) in 1917, just weeks before the US entered World War I. As many as 20,000 locals served, and Puerto Rican soldiers have played a role in every US military conflict since. In many respects, Thanksgiving traditions rooted en la isla are part of a broader military promise: American soldiers always eat well on Thanksgiving Day. Puerto Rican soldiers brought many wartime foodways home with them, and this combined with government subsidies means that today staples can at times feel military-adjacent—especially given the reliance on shelf-stable foods required by a storm-prone island. Over time, the territory’s once agrarian economy (centered around sugar, coffee, and tobacco exports) was transformed into an industrial manufacturing system. Puerto Ricans still consume many foods like tinned corned beef, Vienna sausages, Spam, club soda crackers, and canned vegetables; roughly 85 percent of all food in Puerto Rico is imported.

When Huyke’s father, Hector, served in the Korean War, he encountered the military’s famously bland instant mashed potatoes. From then on, he flat-out refused the dish except during holidays, when Huyke’s mother, Alice (herself a trained cooking instructor), made an impossible-to-resist version: yellow potatoes slowly simmered in cream, enriched with chicken bouillon, then whipped until fluffy with butter. Today a garlicky variation features on Huyke’s Sanguiving table.

Huyke, for her part, wants to steer Puerto Rican cuisine away from processed ingredients and back toward fresh foods—not only because they’re healthier, but also because they are richer in flavor and better convey the layered story of the island’s culinary heritage. She favors from-scratch dishes that lean on regional bounty, from Indigenous staples like maize, peppers, yuca, and other root vegetables to later introductions like plantains and coconuts.

Ají dulce (sweet peppers) are essential to local cuisines across Latin America and the Caribbean—and Chef Giovanna's Sanguiving table.

The best way to explain, she tells me, is to cook together. A few weeks later Huyke joins me in my own kitchen in North Carolina. I quickly learn that cooking alongside her is a lot like having your own personal instructor. At each step she explains how she’s arrived at a certain preparation and why she uses specific ingredients over others. It’s clearly a familiar role: Education remains a central focus for Huyke, and she counts among her mentees young women like Natalia Vallejo, the island’s first James Beard Award–winning chef. She frequently enlists up-and-coming chefs to cook alongside her and makes herself available for mentoring phone calls. I now feel lucky that I can count myself among them.

Although Huyke auditions new Sanguiving dishes every year, Puerto Rican favorites are always on the menu, many of them influenced by her mother’s recipes. Key among them is yuca stuffing—or “estuffing,” as Puerto Ricans commonly pronounce it. Huyke’s family version, Agüeybaná stuffing, is named for the island’s powerful Taíno chief who led the local people at the time of the Spanish invasion in 1493. Huyke peels and then grates fresh yuca before grinding it to a paste in the food processor. Meanwhile, she instructs me to sauté sofrito in olive oil before adding ground and salt pork, annatto, herbs, and aromatics. It’s all piled into a high-walled dish and baked.

Next we turn our attention to pastelón, a lasagna-like layered casserole of fried sweet plantains and creamy queso fresco. The dish was likely born in New York City, where Puerto Rican and Italian communities converged, before finding its way to the island.

“The Puerto Rican and Italian diasporas were physically close in New York during the ’50s—they were exposed to lasagna and mozzarella,” she explains.

Then come more sides. Gandules, or pigeon peas, are a treasured crop. Though they’re frequently served with rice at Sanguiving and other times of year—arroz con gandules is Puerto Rico’s national dish— Huyke instead opts for an escabèche-style salad that marries gandules with tomatoes, avocado, and herbs in a tangy vinaigrette. Another island staple, canned beets, gets a fresh reinterpretation as Huyke roasts a local-grown variety and tops them with crumbled queso fresco.

Huyke’s Sanguiving turkey rests on a banana leaf bed and is adorned with freshly picked wildflowers from the rainforest.

Many Puerto Rican families choose pernil, or roast pork shoulder, as their Sanguiving centerpiece. It is typically marinated overnight in an adobo of minced garlic, sour orange juice, olive oil, oregano, salt, and pepper. But Huyke sticks to turkey, brining it first in a mixture of salt, brown sugar, dried bay leaves, fresh herbs, and peppercorns before pushing butter under the skin and brushing the bird with a blend of rum, melted butter, and guava jelly. Huyke preserves the drippings for a tangy-sweet guava-infused gravy. She also shows me how to make ajilímojilí, a highly adaptable, herbaceous sauce of garlic, ají dulce peppers (similar to bell but fruitier and more delicate), culantro, cilantro, olive oil, vinegar, and her own signature addition: a copious amount of capers. Guests will drizzle it over nearly every dish on her Sanguiving table, she tells me.

After hours of cooking and using every imaginable tool, from a traditional pilón to a modern Vitamix blender, we sit down to enjoy the fruits of our frying, molding, steaming, sautéing, and roasting. The result is unmistakably an American Thanksgiving spread, refracted kaleidoscopically through a fresh, colorful Puerto Rican lens.

Puerto Ricans have both embraced and resisted US imperialism at various points. There always lingers the question of statehood, which exists alongside the island’s long-standing and active independence movement. As Huyke’s cooking demonstrates, this push-pull relationship only continues to play out in all sorts of dynamic ways.

“I believe every cuisine evolves,” she says. “But traditions should be kept and taught. So we do not lose the roots that make us unique.”

#6567. I’ve Finally Found Sunscreens for Oily Skin That Actually Stay Shine-Free

As a beauty editor, sunscreen is a near-daily topic of conversation, practically as commonplace as the weather. But when you have oily skin, finding the right formula isn’t about picking up the next new tube, but finding one that won’t slide off my face; or even worse, one that yields a breakout. Sometimes it feels like I can either protect my skin from UV rays or create a whole new set of skin problems.

Sunscreen remains one of the trickiest skin-care categories to get right when you have oily skin. You want something that protects your skin without feeling greasy, clogging pores, or pilling under makeup; a balance that board-certified dermatologist Marnie Nussbaum, MD knows all too well. “I always tell my patients that oily skin still needs hydration and daily sun protection, but I often get pushback because sunscreens can feel heavy or leave behind a greasy finish for those with oily skin.”

Thankfully, there’s no shortage of options these days, from mineral and chemical filters to tinted and shockingly clear formulas, with finishes ranging from matte to luminous. There’s also an entire world of SPF out there, and I send an eye emoji every time I hear a friend is headed to Paris, Seoul, Tokyo, or Sydney. They know exactly what I’m after.

After plenty of trial and error, I’ve learned to pay close attention to whether a formula is noncomedogenic, meaning it’s designed not to clog pores. I even run ingredient lists through online acne checkers for good measure. Board-certified dermatologist Shereen Teymour, MD, recommends looking for not just non-comedogenic formulas, but ingredients like niacinamide, glycerin, or hyaluronic acid, which can help balance oil production and support the skin barrier without contributing to a greasy feel. “One of the biggest misconceptions is that oily skin does not need hydration,” she explains. “In reality, dehydrated skin can sometimes compensate by producing even more oil.”

Ultimately, the best sunscreens for oily skin offer lightweight textures and comfortable finishes that make you actually want to apply them every day. Below, the formulas I’d recommend, plus how to apply them so you’re glowing, not glistening—and always protected from the sun.

What to Look for in a Sunscreen for Oily Skin

For those with oily skin, board-certified dermatologist Dara Spearman, MD, says the number one thing to look for is a noncomedogenic formula. Dr. Brendan Camp, MD, a double-board-certified dermatologist and dermatopathologist, adds that oil-free, lightweight sunscreens with a mattifying or gel-based texture tend to work best. “A gel-based formula may work better than a heavy cream,” says Spearman. “Some brands even offer liquid sunscreens that dry down to a matte finish, which is ideal for oily skin.”

Should oily skin types use mineral or chemical sunscreens?

It really just depends on your preference. “Oily skin types can use mineral or chemical sunscreens but should look for a lightweight, noncomedogenic formula,” says Camp. However, Spearman suggests opting for mineral formulas, noting that “chemical-based sunscreens can leave skin feeling greasy.”

Can I skip moisturizer and use sunscreen for oily skin?

While it’s always best to experiment and see what works for your skin, Spearman says it’s absolutely fine to skip moisturizer if you’re using a sunscreen that suits your needs. “Doubling up with moisturizer and sunscreen is not necessary for those with oily skin. In fact, I often recommend that my acne-prone patients skip moisturizer in the morning and instead use their medications followed by sunscreen,” she explains. Camp adds that if you do opt to skip moisturizer, make sure your sunscreen offers added skin benefits beyond UV protection. “This might include hydration, skin-barrier support, and antioxidant protection,” he says.

Why does my sunscreen make my face so oily?

“Many sunscreens are composed of emollients or oils to help moisturize the skin and improve spreadability,” Spearman explains. “This can make facial skin, which naturally has more oil glands, appear even oilier.” She also notes that some barrier sunscreens can trap sebum or natural oils on the skin’s surface, which contributes to a greasy look. Camp adds that products made with emollient or occlusive ingredients are more likely to trap oil, while lightweight liquid or gel-based sunscreens tend to leave a more matte finish.

How to Wear Sunscreen Without Looking Greasy

If greasiness is one of your main concerns, look for a matte-based physical sunscreen in either a liquid or gel formula or one with a naturally mattifying finish. Camp recommends ingredients like niacinamide, silica, and zinc—all of which may help reduce shine. Another option, according to Spearman, is to skip moisturizer altogether and consider using a powder-based sunscreen for reapplication throughout the day.

When we test and review a product, we take a holistic approach to deliver well-rounded product recommendations. First, we lean on Vogue’s vast network of experts—from board-certified dermatologists to celebrity aestheticians—to gain professional acumen on the industry’s standout products, ones these specialists would actually use on their clients. We pair their expertise with our editorial best practices to curate the thoughtful edits you read on our site.

As it relates to sunscreens for oily skin, we selected the best based on the following characteristics: ingredients, texture, finish, SPF level, UV filters, broad-spectrum coverage, and the skin-care concerns they address. To do this, we paired our own personal tests of each formula with expert guidance and reviewer insights to determine which we would recommend to you. Read more about our testing methodology here.

#6564. Apple Juice Bread

A simple swap from water to apple juice transforms this basic bread recipe into a subtly sweet loaf that is perfect to tear into at breakfast time with a smear of good butter on top, but it also takes a PB&J to the next level. The subtle, but unmistakable, undercurrent of apple sweetness struck me as a bit of a magic trick in a bread that, otherwise, to the eye and hand was just a soft white loaf.

I first encountered the idea at the small four-seat teppanyaki restaurant in the back of the Suiran Hotel in Kyoto, Japan, where chef Tsubasa Yamaguchi served it before my first course; it was a perfect way to start the meal. When I asked him what he did differently to prepare it, he said he just took the same rustic bread recipe he baked elsewhere and used apple juice in place of water. I was incredulous. That was it? The same amount? The same technique? Yes and yes, he said. I was hooked. It turns out the water-to-juice switcheroo gives an added taste of fall without taking anything away from the shape and texture. It’s become an instant favorite at my house both breakfast and lunch, and I expect it will be at yours.

Take care when you’re lowering the bread into the Dutch oven; it is a slightly nerve-wracking moment but a little attention is all that’s needed. You can do it!

More apple recipes here: 37 Apple Desserts That Make Us Want to Pick the Whole Orchard

Mix 4 cups (500 g) all-purpose flour, 1¾ cups apple juice, 1 Tbsp. Diamond Crystal or 1¾ tsp. Morton kosher salt, 1 Tbsp. sugar, and one ¼-oz. envelope instant yeast (about 2¼ tsp.) in a large bowl just until flour is hydrated and a very shaggy dough forms, about 1 minute. Cover bowl with plastic wrap and let dough sit at room temperature 15 minutes.

Set a small bowl of room-temperature water on work surface for easy reaching. Uncover dough, dip your hand in water and stretch one side of dough up and over to meet opposite side; turn bowl 90°. Repeat 3 more times, turning bowl 90° after each fold. (This constitutes 1 full fold.) If dough doesn’t always stretch to meet opposite side, just aim for the middle. Wet your hands and shake off excess water any time dough begins to feel sticky. Cover dough and let sit 30 minutes (set a timer). Repeat folding process to make 1 full fold. Re-cover and let dough sit another 30 minutes. Repeat folding process and resting one more time. By the last fold, dough should be significantly smoother and tighter.

Transfer dough to a generously floured surface, dust with flour, and shape into a tight ball. Dust dough with more flour. Dust a kitchen towel with flour and place inside a high-sided bowl to line. Arrange dough, seam side up, in bowl on top of towel. Tightly cover bowl with plastic wrap and let dough sit in a warm spot until puffy, about 45 minutes.

Place a rack in middle of oven, then set a large ovenproof Dutch oven with a lid on it; preheat oven to 400°. Place a 12" square of parchment paper on a flat surface. Cut a 2"-long slit in each corner toward the center. Very carefully, tip dough out onto center of parchment, trying your best not to deflate it or ruin its shape. (It’s easiest to place parchment on a flat plate so you can easily turn dough out of bowl.) Working very quickly and using a pair of kitchen shears lightly coated in vegetable oil, cut an X in center of bread. Remove pot from oven and very carefully lower dough into pot. Cover pot and return to oven.

Bake bread 35 minutes. Uncover pot, reduce oven temperature to 375°, and continue to bake bread until crust is deeply browned, 35–40 minutes more. Carefully tip loaf out onto a wire rack and let cool at least 1 hour before slicing.

Do Ahead: Bread can be baked 3 days ahead. Let cool completely; store airtight at room temperature.

#6563. This Harvest Caesar Salad Is The Fall Side Everyone Asks Me To Bring

My love for Caesar salad knows no bounds, but in the fall, this harvest version is a STAPLE in my rotation. I first made it for a Friendsgiving last year, and people loved it so much that I ended up making it for my own Thanksgiving and Christmas celebrations, too. Every time, friends and family begged me for the recipe—it’s that good.

The best thing about it? It only requires a couple of easy ingredient upgrades to turn the classic salad into a fall favorite—here’s what makes it truly special.

As you’ve probably realized, this isn’t your plain Jane Caesar salad. There are two easy swaps that make this salad a side dish star. First, instead of romaine as the base, this salad lets kale shine. If you’re not a kale fan, stay with me. Once it’s massaged down with lemon juice and salt, it becomes perfectly tender and downright delicious—it’s the ideal hearty base for this salad.

The second and most important swap? Instead of sourdough croutons, this salad roasts pieces of butternut squash on a bed of freshly shredded Parm to create crispy frico squash “croutons.” As soon as I removed the tray from the oven and started breaking up the cheesy squash pieces, I had to remind myself that I couldn’t eat them all on their own—at least a few had to actually go in the salad.

This salad requires a few extra steps, but they’re quick and well worth it. First, make the Caesar dressing and refrigerate it until you’re ready to assemble. If you don’t have the time, a store-bought dressing will do just fine.

While that’s chilling, you’ll prepare the butternut squash croutons by cutting up your squash, shredding some Parm on an oiled baking sheet (don't use the pre-shredded kind—it just won’t melt the same), placing your squash on top, and baking until the cheese is crisp and browned on the bottom.

After you massage the kale with lemon and salt (don’t be stingy here—put those muscles to good use), all that’s left is to assemble! I highly recommend assembling in stages—dressing with the kale, then half the squash and Parmesan—before serving with the rest of the squash, Parmesan, and remaining dressing on the side for anyone who prefers more dressing than salad (again, guilty!).

#6562. 10 Airbnbs in Sweden for a Stylish Winter Getaway

For all the lakeside escapades and long, light-filled days of Scandi summer, something about winter in Sweden feels especially apropos. True, the sun is basically a missing person until April; but between the Christmas markets, the reindeer running loose in the northern part of the country, the sauna traditions, and the copious amounts of glögg being poured at cafés, it’s about as cozy and festive as it gets. (Provided, of course, you pack the right layers.)

Experience all this up close is by booking an Airbnb; whether it’s an apartment on the outskirts of Stockholm or a quiet escape that’s significantly more remote, a home of your own is the best way to truly get a feel for this special time of year.

Try an 18th-century cottage surrounded by fields and wetlands for brisk winter walks; or perhaps a colorful jewel box apartment right in Stockholm (complete with a terrace, if you’re willing to brave the cold for your morning coffee). We even found a cabin on your very own personal island; if you want to go truly off the grid, WiFi-free and everything, it’s the vacation rental for you.

Keep reading for our favorite Airbnbs in Sweden to book this winter.

Located in Midsommarkransen, a residential neighborhood dotted with boutiques and cafés, this bright studio does color well. From pine-green limewash in the bedroom to terracotta-colored windows, it’s the antidote to winter blues—it even has a large balcony. (Admittedly, a less-tempting amenity in the winter months; but if you’re feeling brave enough to take your mug of glögg al fresco, the twinkle lights set a cozy scene.)

Known for its farm shops selling local delicacies and small fishing villages, Österlen is a great option for your Swedish trip. Set the scene for your stay with this cozy home. It dates back to 1901, with soaring ceilings and whitewashed wood panels that make it feel even more spacious than it is. It comes with four bikes you can use for the duration of your stay—in more temperate months, cycle out to one of the aforementioned farm stands for dinner ingredients.

Amenities: Bicycle rental, washer, piano, record player, exercise equipment, wood-burning fireplace, hammock, outdoor furniture, backyard

This two-bedroom home is waterfront living at its finest. Designed by an architecture, it sits on the contemporary side with brutalist-like concrete walls and floor-to-ceiling windows. Rent a car to explore the archipelago—you’ll be near both Stockholm and the beaches for day trips.

Amenities: Washer, TV, grill, outdoor dining, pool, free parking

The coastal town of Landskrona has a lot to offer, not least of all this unique property. Part-historic landmark, part-vacation rental, this 18th-century “Fortification House” is deceptively large (it can actually sleep six people) and full of charm. Antique furnishings and high ceilings give it a stately feel, with plenty of decor ideas to bookmark—starting with the lace canopy curtains in the bedroom. Want to bring back a piece of your holiday? All the furniture in the apartment is actually for sale; inquire within to purchase.

Amenities: Washer/dryer, TV, sound system, fire pit, outdoor space, grill, shared boat slip, shared outdoor pool available seasonally, housekeeping available at a cost

Vacation amongst the locals in this sunny cabin on Lidingö, an affluent island on the Stockholm archipelago. The house itself is bright and well-equipped, with architectural details like stained glass and barrel-vaulted wood ceilings to take note of. The biggest draw, however, is its location: You’ll be steps from the beach, which takes on a more rugged form in the winter months, and a wood-fired sauna is within walking distance.

Amenities: Washer/dryer, outdoor dining, free parking

You get city and country all wrapped up in one with this circa-1910s home, which is just outside of the center of Stockholm. It has seven beds and a sunny garden, with several family-friendly amenities like a travel crib that’s available upon request and a large outdoor dining table for meals at home. Inside, cozy details put you instantly at ease. From the plant-lined windowsills to the roomy clawfoot tub in the bathroom, you’ll feel like you’re staying at your stylish friends’ house.

Amenities: Washer, HDTV, piano, Bluetooth sound system, indoor fireplace, outdoor furniture, pets allowed

It’s not every day you get the chance to stay in a renovated chapel. This house, located on the island of Gotland, offers you the opportunity: Originally a 1912 Baptist church, it’s now a well-decorated vacation rental that’s a great size for a large group. It sleeps up to eight, with a main house and a guest house on the property. When you’re feeling stir-crazy, the nearest beach is a quick two-kilometer bike ride away.

Amenities: Washer, TV, ping pong table, indoor fireplace, backyard, grill, private pool

For a lakeside vacation, book this home. It’s right near Siljan, one of the country’s largest lakes, and sleeps five with use of the large sofa in the living room. Inside, Scandinavian design elements steal the show. Expect colorful gingham bedding, paper lanterns, and even a traditional Swedish fireplace to warm up by—you may just leave scheming to redesign your own home.

Amenities: TV, high chair, outdoor dining

For an outlandishly extravagant holiday, go all out and book your very own island. (Which isn’t actually as extravagant as it sounds: This cabin goes for less than $200 a night.) Welcome to Aurora Isle, a tiny island in northern Sweden’s Västerbotten where this sweet cottage is the only thing around—except for a wood-fired sauna, of course.

This spot is ideal for the couple willing to get a bit adventurous: There’s no electricity or running water here (the lamps are solar-powered), so you get to fully lean in to an off-the-grid experience. Get around with the property’s small boat, cook all your meals outside, and spend evenings stargazing—in the winter, you can even see the Northern Lights.

Amenities: Outdoor shower, firepit, grill, pet-friendly

Situate yourself in Nyköping, the capital of the castle-riddled region of Sörmland in southeastern Sweden, in this cozy cottage. It’s from the 18th century but has been beautifully restored: Mauve toile wallpaper, two wood-burning fireplaces, and a gorgeous, fully equipped kitchen (which even comes with a bread maker) are among its highlights. Step outside to the private garden in the morning to take your coffee in the fresh air.

Amenities: Washer, Bluetooth sound system, wood-burning fireplace, backyard, outdoor furniture, grill, pet-friendly

#6561. 15 Best Colognes for Men in 2026, Staff-Tested and Reviewed

In 2026, the best colognes for men go beyond just smelling good, though first things first: They should smell incredible. A great fragrance nowadays tells a story, and if you choose wisely, can become part of your personal lore. I, for one, am a fragrance obsessive and will spritz a cologne at home with nowhere to be, purely for morale. What's more, years of testing and writing about fragrances has taught me just how effortlessly a stellar composition can lift your entire day, whether it’s a mainstream designer release, a niche luxury creation, or something decidedly indie.

My work in the fragrance field has also taught me that while some guys find one signature scent and ride with it for decades; others prefer a variety for different moods, seasons, and days where first impressions matter. To help you figure out where you stand, I tapped the GQ staffers who wear more fragrance in a year than most men do in a lifetime. Collectively, we put old-money classics, cult favorites, and new heat through their atomizers, looking for scents that feel distinctive and deserve repeat wear. The final cut includes a bevy of choices for all occasions, from heritage heavyweights like Acqua di Parma Colonia to future signatures like D.S. & Durga's I Don't Know What. Here's to the sweet smell of success.

Le Labo has no shortage of heavy hitters, from the omnipresent Santal 33 to newer standouts like Eucalyptus 20, but few recent launches have built buzz quite like Thé Matcha 26. Much of its insider appeal lies in its earthy yet fresh, smoky yet subtle, almost Zen-like character. Green fig leads the opening, paired with a calming tea accord, while bitter orange adds a bright bite. As it settles, the fragrance takes on a woodier, herbal edge, with a soft, green haze that runs throughout. A skin scent at heart and undeniably hip, it’s become a modern staple for Le Labo’s more discerning devotees.

Staff Notes: “I’ve been wearing Le Labo’s Thé Matcha for a few years now, and it has become my go-to. As someone who has a hard time finding a scent that doesn't give me a headache or feels too strong throughout the day, it’s one of those rare scents that just works. It has a clean, almost airy quality to it that immediately settles into something effortless and fresh.” —Bowen Fernie, senior visuals editor

Malin+Goetz is one of the few names that began in skincare and went on to make genuinely excellent, indie-cool fragrances, all at very accessible prices. The apothecary vibes run deep, from the formulas to those glass deco bottles that ooze medicine-cabinet chic. The brand's Leather EDP—like my favorite from the line, Cannabis—doesn’t smell exactly like its name. In classic M+G fashion, it plays more of a supporting role here, blended with pepper and clove for a bit of kick. Lily and orchid create a fresh floral heart, while violet adds a velvety depth, all grounded by creamy sandalwood and cedar. And of course, that warm, comforting leather note wears like a Perfecto. It’s a gorgeous spring-ready daily driver, with a grassy floral vibe that plays beautifully against the grain.

Staff Notes: “From the perfect broken-in leather jacket to a leather sofa that's been with you move after move, there's something about the smell of well-loved cowhide that's so damn captivating. Malin+Goetz captured that feeling in a bottle with its Leather EDP. The cologne brings in cedarwood and sandalwood with orchid just to avoid any possibilities of your scent being compared to a vintage store.” —Tyler Chin, associate commerce editor

Is there any cologne more synonymous with men’s cologne, period, than Polo Ralph Lauren? Since 1978, it has helped define what “classically good” smells like and sits firmly planted in the pantheon of modern perfumery. Anything that iconic will have its detractors, but it’s embedded in the culture for a reason, and few colognes today are as recognizable. Even with reformulations over the years, that signature woody aromatic structure still hits, with juniper berry and bergamot up top for brightness, coriander and a blend of herbs bringing spice, touches of florals, and leather for depth—along with that unmistakable pine accord humming throughout. Woody, aromatic, and classic, it’s a cologne guys will always rock.

Staff Notes: “Smelling good is paramount to success as a modern man. (Just ask my close personal friend Ralph Lauren.) Woody, aromatic, and a little spicy, this is a classic scent that's always on top of my dresser.” —Matthew Roberson, staff writer

It’s a household name, a modern icon, and still one of the most sophisticated yet approachable colognes you can wear pretty much anywhere. Created by Chanel’s famed nose, Jacques Polge, more than 15 years ago, Bleu de Chanel remains as singular and versatile today as ever. It opens bright with grapefruit and lemon, sharpened by a hint of fresh mint, before a heart of spicy ginger, warming nutmeg, and heady jasmine. Then comes the MVP lineup of woods: cedar, vetiver, sandalwood, patchouli, and labdanum, all working together in the citrus-spice harmony that defines this blue-hued gem. Flankers have followed, but the OG Bleu de Chanel is inimitable.

Staff Notes: “I keep a travel-sized bottle of this in my Dopp kit at all times. It's classic, great for every season, and super versatile when it comes to occasion—its citrus notes and woody base make it equally good for work dinners, poolside piña coladas, and stoking the fire outside your glamping cabin.” —Ian Burke, senior commerce editor

Baccarat Rouge 540 is now an olfactory cultural landmark. You’ve absolutely smelled this socialite-signature wafting through the night, whether from the backseat of an Uber Black or across a dimly lit dinner table downtown. Some fragrances get so popular they tip into fatigue territory, but 540 earned its status for a reason. First, it comes from one of the most meticulous noses in the game. Second, the scent speaks for itself: an intoxicating, sweet floral amber, with saffron adding a subtle spice, jasmine bringing warmth, and a heavy dose of amberwood creating that signature glowing aura, all balanced by soft woods. Polarizing, yes, but anything that moves the needle tends to follow its own rhythm, and 540 is a modern classic via its own design.

Staff Notes: “Francis Kurkdjian's reputation-making Baccarat Rouge might not be the buzziest scent on the market anymore, but it's definitely the ritziest. If you don't want to smell like a perpetually fapitzed Upper East Side doyenne, you, friend, should reconsider a lot more than just your scent profile.” — Avidan Grossman, senior commerce editor

YSL has no shortage of effortlessly elegant colognes, from more mainstream, accessible options to elevated releases in the Le Vestiaire Des Parfums collection, all infused with that unmistakable YSL panache. On paper, Trench reads as a citrus floral, but in wear, it’s laced with soft, musky undertones that give it an airy, slightly edgy feel. It opens with tangerine and bergamot, layered over heady iris and fresh neroli, before settling into a warm base of musk and cedar. A fig note threads through it all, adding a subtly sweet, verdant hue. Citrusy and floral but grounded in musk, with a slightly funky undertone (the good kind), it’s a chic fragrance you can wear from sun-soaked afternoons in the park straight into date night and out into the cool, tastefully debaucherous night beyond.

Staff Notes: “If you were to bottle the feeling of a perfect Parisian night, it would smell like YSL Trench: heady, sleek, and just a little dangerous.” —Tyler Sparling, contributing market editor

Eau de Minthé is one of the more distinctive entries in Diptyque’s GOAT-level catalog, a cooling blend of mint and patchouli that reads as a fresh, green fougère with a retro ’80s and ’90s edge, albeit very au courant. The mint is fresh and slightly spicy, far from anything toothpaste-adjacent, layered with warm nutmeg, sweet geranium, and a soft, velvety rose. It’s a cologne I wouldn’t have immediately associated with the house, until the drydown, anchored by that signature Diptyque patchouli, brings depth and candle-flickering craftsmanship the brand does so uniquely well. Fresh, aromatic, and with a bit of nostalgia baked in, this is a layered gem to wear for all your mint julep-fueled warm-weather soirées.

Staff Notes: "Diptyque's Eau de Minthé is what I imagine Michelin-level mixologists aspire toward when they're crafting their cocktails. At first sniff, it's garden-fresh floral notes are uplifted with subtle minty notes before settling into deep patchouli notes that give it a well-rounded experience that's equally light and grounding." —Gerald Ortiz, style commerce writer

To me, Tom Ford has four all-timers in his Private Blend canon: Oud Wood, Neroli Portofino, Tuscan Leather, and the sultry tobacco-vanilla duality that is Tobacco Vanille. When this spicy, warm gourmand landed in 2007, it helped redefine what a tobacco fragrance could smell like. The note historically skewed fringe or overtly macho, but Ford, of course, reframed it as chic and decadent, pairing rich tobacco leaf with vanilla, ginger, cocoa, woods, and dried fruits. The signature aroma is plush and addictive, with a near-edible warmth that never tips into excess, as sweet vanilla and spice slowly bloom through the drydown. It’s a masterclass in softening a once-polarizing note into something smooth, inviting, and alluring, and still one of the house’s most widely admired scents today.

Staff Notes: “What's not to love about Tobacco Vanille? It's smooth, smoky, sexy, and just the right amount of sweet. Far better than smoking an actual cigarette—and more luxurious, too.” — Trishna Rikhy, associate social media manager

Musc Ravageur has a devoted following, with fans reaching for this alluring, sultry, spiced gem as both a signature scent and for date nights alike. Released in 2000, it helped usher musk (as a note) into a broader, chicer tier of perfumery. The composition is beautifully layered, opening with herbal lavender, spicy coriander, and a hint of bright citrus before melting into clove and a heady rose, all resting on a rich base of musk, vanilla, tonka, amber, and patchouli. Besides being a benchmark for animalic gourmands, it’s one of the most intricately composed scents out there, where, if you read the pyramid, you can pick out each note as it unfolds. We fragrance fanatics love that.

Staff Notes: "This isn't called an icon by accident. I keep coming back to Musc Ravageur year after year. One spray of the warm vanilla, spiced cinnamon, perfectly balanced with clean musk is all it takes for pure chemistry. This is the kind of scent that turns heads." —Reginald Christian, commerce director

London-based Perfumer H has carved out its own unique path, from its apothecary-meets-indie-meets-luxury vibe to its often one-word, subtle creations that smell distinctive yet approachable. Ink is a case in point. As a self-proclaimed bookworm, I was already sold on its inspiration: late nights spent in dimly lit libraries. But the scent itself is an intriguing study, weaving together woods, papyrus (because paper, of course), heady rose, spice, warm ambers, and an incense-like, meditative quality. The result is an addictive, page-turning woody floral composition that feels both cerebral and wearable, the kind of fragrance you rock when you're quite possibly the coolest dude in the room—and likely the most well-read, too.

Staff Notes: “Perfumer H pretty much had me at their tagline: Making Air Visible. But then I smelled Ink, and was completely seduced. It transports me to lamp-lit reading rooms and old-world ateliers. And even better, because it's so light, I can apply it multiple times a day.” —Louis Cheslaw, contributing commerce editor

Well before skin scents became a thing, the indie aromatic heavyweights at D.S. & Durga dropped their now cult-classic I Don’t Know What Eau de Parfum in the late 2010s. It is less a traditional fragrance and more of an enhancer (though for many, it is the main aromatic event). The polar opposite of beast-mode projection, subtlety is its byword, with a verdant, woody air scent you lean in to experience rather than one that announces itself across a room. Iso E Super, a versatile synthetic aroma chemical known for its longevity and velvety skin-like texture, does most of the heavy, or rather light, lifting, blended with bergamot, vetiver, and sandalwood to create one of the best fresh skin scents of all time. Wear it on its own or use it to boost and layer with other fragrances. I don’t know what else to say; it all works.

Staff Notes: “I Don’t Know What has a gentle and clean scent that feels like a whisper compared to more bombastic fragrances out there. The light citrusy hit of bergamot is exactly what I need when layering scents during the warmer parts of the year.” —Jordan Bowman, commerce editor

One of the genre’s most renowned reference vetivers, this Guerlain classic has influenced not just every vetiver cologne, but many fragrances today, period. The composition is less the smoky, rooty side of the note and more early-morning, dewy freshness, clean and crisp, with just enough (good dirty) earthiness underneath to keep it interesting. Citrus and spice lift the opening before it settles into a grassy core, rounded out by touches of tobacco and woods. More than any grand concept, it smells like stepping outside early in the morning, when everything still feels a little cool, damp, and alive. With longevity and that timeless cologne feel, it has remained a benchmark since its 1950 debut and a signature scent for so many.

Staff Notes: “This bottle has been in my rotation for a few years, and it’s a benchmark for anyone into fresh, verdant scents. To my nose, it’s always smelled of drinking a Negroni in a five-star hotel room, or someplace equally polished. I spritz it particularly in the colder months whenever I’m set to meet new people, because I find it's an easy way to make a good first impression.” —Michael Nolledo, commerce director

So many folks whose taste I admire wear Colonia. Endlessly polished and easy to wear, it’s about as close as it gets to a perfect daily driver. First introduced in 1916, the Italian icon still feels as relevant today as it did over a century ago, built on that signature blend of citrus, herbs, and woods, wearing its subtlety and old-world refinement on its (freshly pressed) sleeve. The opening is citrus crisp, before settling into herbaceous notes of lavender, rosemary, and vetiver over a smooth base of patchouli, sandalwood, and soft amber warmth. It carries that classic barbershop fougère-meets-Italian-citrus-grove energy, a cologne your dad (and his dad) wore to work and date nights alike—but that smells just as fresh on you today.

Staff Notes: “'It's hard to pick the perfect cologne for the office’ is something I might say if I'd never smelled this bottle of Acqua di Parma. It smells like biting into a sexy tangerine, but in an inoffensive way that won't raise any eyebrows in your desk clump." —Doug Guida, social producer

Every exemplary fragrance house has a defining undercurrent. With Aesop (who's just as well known for its scents as its skincare), it's a botanical, earthy, elevated thread running through those amber-hued bottles. Rōzu Eau de Parfum is a woody, aromatic, rose-forward composition, not of the sweet or traditional variety, but for those who appreciate richer, headier takes. Rose, alongside iris, is one of my favorite floral notes, and here it's handled with nuance, pairing the dewy, velvety accord with a lift of citrus, then grounding it with sandalwood for creaminess, guaiac wood for incense-leaning flourishes, and vetiver for earthiness. A jasmine accord adds depth to the green, earthy rose aroma—another indie homerun from the Aussie house.

Staff Notes: “I thought I wasn’t a rose-cologne person, but then Aesop mixed in some shiso and jasmine, and it was love at first whiff. Rōzu (the Japanese pronunciation of the English word “rose”), is my go-to when I want a unisex scent that’ll last just a bit longer than the work day, because I don’t want to be That Cologne Wearer at the gym.” —Mari Herrema, marketing and production manager

Perhaps no cologne is as referenced, memed, reviewed, and well-known in modern mainstream fragrance culture as Sauvage. The line can get a little confusing, but it all comes back to a core DNA built on citrus, pepper, and ambroxan, just pushed in different directions. The EDT is ultra-fresh, the EDP adds warmth, and the Parfum goes denser. Then there’s Elixir, the darker, spicier, more aromatic outlier. It’s my favorite of the group, leaning into evening territory with nutmeg and cinnamon bringing gourmand warmth, grapefruit adding lift, and classic lavender giving it that fougère backbone, all resting on a heady base of amber, patchouli, sandalwood, and a subtly sweet licorice accord. Elixir is the refined, yet still slightly mischievous side of Sauvage—spicy, warm, fresh, and it smells good on pretty much everyone.

Staff Notes: “I was gifted a bottle of Dior Sauvage, I think, to give to a man in my life. But I love men's colognes so I decided to keep it for myself. When winter rolled around, I gave it a try and I noticed pretty immediately that the scent had pull. (I got the most interest from an Uber driver who was terribly into my fragrance until I told him it wasn't for women.) Somehow it gave me that fresh-out-of-the-shower burst of energy while also smelling woody, warm, and sexy—perfect for cooler days. I'm happy I didn't give it away.” —Savannah Sobrevilla, associate editor

The fragrances above are all GQ staffer favorites, and I worked closely with the team to bring to life what makes each one worthy of a spot in your olfactory arsenal. Of course, scent is wildly subjective. One person's all-time favorite daily driver might leave someone else scrunching their nose. Tomato, tomahto. That's part of the fun, after all. No universal crowd-pleaser exists, and what smells incredible on one guy might not work for the next.

Now, here's where I get to shine a light on a few personal favorites. From modern classics to under-the-radar niche gems and newer fumes, these are the colognes I love right now, along with a few I think deserve more attention, spanning a range of price points. Consider this a little extra olfactory inspiration, courtesy of yours truly.

I've smelled pretty much everything indie-luxe stalwart Byredo has put out over the years (including the new, fantastic Future Memories), but it wasn't until recently that I finally got my nose on Oud Immortel. It brings together just about every cold-weather note I adore, from oud and smoky incense to earthy patchouli, moss, and tobacco, weaving them into something sultry and almost decadent. But there's also that signature Byredo airiness, an almost skin-scent-like softness that keeps it from feeling too dense or overpowering.

When I first experienced Terre d'Hermès years ago, it immediately became a staple in my rotation. It's one of the best designer colognes ever, and I was, and still am, obsessed with its woody, citrusy elegance. But while the original is best suited to cooler months, with Eau Intense Vétiver, you've got an equally chic, warm-weather counterpart.

French grooming favorite Horace knows how to make fragrances that smell like they should cost far more. Inspired by Freddie Mercury's legendary 41st birthday bash at Ibiza's Pikes Hotel in 1987, this is one intriguing aromatic. The name sounds summery, but to my nose, it's more like a winter holiday celebration, with crisp fir balsam and cypress lending an evergreen character.

I’ve been intrigued by New York-based Vilhelm Parfumerie for years, right down to those distinctive bottles shaped like miniature decanters, and Morning Chess is so, so smooth. It’s a blend of citrus and amber you don’t come across often: fresh and bright on the surface, just like the morning, but a few swift chess moves later, it settles into a regal, leathery warmth with an earthy undercurrent. Checkmate.

I’m a big fan of buzzy Brooklyn house Rite of Way, as all three (yes, just three) of its fragrances are so wonderfully indie and cool. I’m normally not one for aquatics, but its inaugural scent, Outer Realm, won me over by pairing citrus and marine notes with incense to create a scent that’s anything but banal. Citron and grapefruit bring a sharp, juicy brightness, while sea spray and lotus lend an airy, almost otherworldly quality. Then, as it settles, amber emerges, giving the composition a warmth you don't typically associate with aquatics.

Quentin Bisch is one of the most renowned and daring perfumers working today, and to my nose, he has a way with woods, giving them a richness and depth that's become a calling card. His Bois Impérial for Essential Parfums, a niche house known for making high-quality fragrances more accessible, has become a sensation on fragrance forums, and for good reason. Built around Akigalawood, a patchouli-derived ingredient with a rich woody character, it has a spicy, peppery bite, while an invigorating freshness keeps it from veering too heavy.

Los Angeles–based Perfumehead’s exemplary Canadian Tuxedo reminds me of my childhood on Long Beach Island: Evening light dancing off the driftwood, when everything felt quiet, introspective, and creatively stirring. On paper, it sits in the amber family, but it wears like a meeting of resinous woods and coastal air, lifted by bitter orange leaf and coriander. As it settles, the fragrance takes on a warm, herbal quality with a touch of spice and a soft, musky finish that feels almost windswept.

I respect the citrus fragrance family immensely, but as a leading note, it’s never been my everyday go-to. L’Or de Louis completely reframed it for me: a citrus shaped by smoke and gourmand tones that’s become a fixture in my olfactory arsenal. Aromatic indie heavyweights Arquiste have a knack for weaving history into their fragrances, and this one takes us to Louis XIV’s Versailles, where bonfires burned near citrus trees at the Grand Orangery. The gold flecks in the bottle are another nod to its grandiose inspiration, resembling, to me, little flickers of fire suspended in the glass.

I recently watched a podcast where Sarah Sherman lamented that she could no longer get her hands on Santa Maria Novella's Patchouli. That's the kind of attachment people develop to the centuries-old Florentine house, helped also by its gorgeous bottles. I like Opoponax: a honeyed resin with a smoky, incense-like quality. Think monks in cloisters, holy water, dimly lit chapels, and quiet garden courtyards.

Even as Icelandic house Fischersund gains serious attention stateside, it still feels like the cool kid in the room, with a noir-leaning sensibility and music and art woven into its indie DNA. I adore No. 23, the flagship scent, which opens dark and smoky, almost charred, before softening into resinous woods, spice, and a hint of sweet citrus with a faint animalic undercurrent.

It's not often I get to shine a light on a gem in Creed's storied catalog that isn't one of its many heavy hitters, but Bois du Portugal is a bit of a slept-on classic that currently has me hooked. An old-school gentleman's fougère, it's fresh, woody, spicy, and above all aromatic, built from little more than bergamot, a hefty dose of lavender, and a blend of woods and patchouli—proof that a few top-quality elements, blended exceptionally well, can speak volumes. Created in 1987, it still smells every bit as relevant today.

Iberian Leather isn't for beginners; it's the kind of scent you have to vibe with to appreciate its artistry and complexity. A richly layered fragrance, it feels like wandering through a damp, historic castle as aged wood, worn leather, and the scent of nearby flower beds wafts through the night air. And the bottle is flat-out stunning, too, looking like something straight out of Game of Thrones.

Ever wondered about the difference between an “EDT” and an “EDP?” It's not actually all that complicated. The primary differentiator comes down to the percentage of perfumed oils used in the product, which dictates how brands classify their scents. These days, we tend to treat “cologne” as a catchall term for any men’s fragrance, but technically speaking, the term is just one of many you should know about. These are the rest.

The classifications above aren't an exact science, of course, but the concentration levels they allude to are a solid indicator of where to set your expectations, and how much a fragrance will cost.

Colognes right now have more personality than ever, and more and more gentlemen are moving beyond the one-bottle approach. Plenty of guys still swear by a signature scent, but many are building rotations based on budget, mood, and setting. As Jake Levy and Matt Belanger, founders of NYC fragrance shop Stéle, told us, “Today folks want variety: one to go out, one to go to work, one for date night, and even one to start a conversation.”

If you’re starting from scratch, keep it simple: start with two bottles—one clean, versatile daily driver and one with a little more edge for nights out. From there, add by season or occasion, like say, something fresh and citrusy for warm weather, something woody or spicy for when the temps drop.

Keep this in mind, too: classic fragrance families like citrus, woods, gourmand, and floral will always have a place, but modern perfumery is more wide-open than ever. As Carlos Huber of Arquiste puts it, if you love smoky oud or animalic leather, there’s no reason it can’t be your best cologne. Wear what fits your aura, not your algorithm.

As one of GQ’s regular fragrance writers, I’ve spent years testing colognes and reporting on the category, while the wider shopping team has spent an inordinate amount of time thinking about what deserves space on a shelf. Together, we cast a wide net, considering household names, indie favorites, heritage heavyweights, and artisanal imprints.

Because not every guy wears cologne the same way, or for the same reasons, we pay close attention to context and budget. We test scents on skin over full days of wear, tracking how they opened, dried down, projected, and lasted over time. Some needed to work at the office, others on date nights, others as an everyday signature. Each winning pick was judged on scent quality, longevity, versatility, and price, along with the simplest test of all: whether we actually wanted to keep spraying it.

The result is a list that reflects a range of tastes, occasions, and price points—from tried-and-true stalwarts to modern disruptors, affordable go-tos to wildly expensive (but wildly worth-it) flexes.

#6559. 10 Gnocchi Skillet Weeknight Dinners For Any Craving Or Time Of Year

All you need is one pan and less than an hour.

In our eyes, the hallmark of a great weeknight dinner is gnocchi. The comforting, pillowy pasta is the perfect vessel for endless sauces and flavor combinations, making it a star no matter the season or craving. Another bonus? In many of our favorite gnocchi dinners, there’s no need to cook the gnocchi beforehand. That means no waiting for water to boil or dirtying extra dishes. These 10 gnocchi skillet dinners bring all of your favorite flavors together in one pan, and all in under an hour. Simply put, gnocchi is made for weeknights.

A dirty martini happens to be the perfect template to turn into a savory recipe and we’ve riffed in many ways.? This dirty martini gnocchi is our latest attempt to transform the iconic drink into dinner, and we have to admit—it’s a success.

This is a true 30-minute meal, and it calls for ingredients that you might already have on hand. Like our other Marry Me dishes, this saucy one-pan dinner features a base of fresh garlic, sun-dried tomatoes, thyme, heavy cream, and Parmesan tossed with pillowy-soft and quick-cooking gnocchi, then topped with a pinch of red pepper flakes for a little extra spicy kick.

Creamy Pumpkin Gnocchi With Italian Sausage

For this creamy gnocchi dinner, we added pumpkin to create a comforting, nutty, and slightly sweet sauce that pairs perfectly with pillowy gnocchi and Italian sausage.

Out of all the party dips, spinach and artichoke reigns supreme in our book, so we turned it into this decadent pasta dish. We combined everything we love about our favorite dip—spinach, artichokes, cream & cheese—with quick-cooking gnocchi, turning it into an easy meatless dinner that’s loaded with flavor.

Every year, this chicken dinner is one of our most-loved recipes—it's not hard to see why. We paired chicken breasts with pillowy gnocchi in a creamy sauce, complete with mushrooms and spinach, all in one pan for easy cleanup.

In this new take on one of our most-popular dinners (creamy chicken & gnocchi), chicken breast cutlets are seasoned, pan-seared, then smothered in smoky, creamy spinach and mushroom sauce alongside plump gnocchi. It gets added flair from crumbled feta, ras el hanout, and spicy harissa paste—a North African hot sauce.

One of our most-popular dinners, this one-pan chicken bacon gnocchi is a weeknight favorite for very good reason. The creation of this dish all started with our one-pan chicken & gnocchi, which is so well-loved, we decided to upgrade it with one of our favorite ingredients: crispy bacon!

Let the good times roll because tonight’s dinner takes you down South to the cuisine of Louisiana with this chicken and pasta skillet. Just like our other gnocchi skillet dinners, this one is absolutely craveable; plus, it brings all the flavors we associate with New Orleans into your kitchen.

When developing this recipe, we took inspiration from the winning flavor profile of our Caprese chicken gnocchi soup, but anyone familiar with classic Caprese knows the basic formula: fresh mozzarella, tomatoes, basil, olive oil, and balsamic vinegar. In this recipe, We’re adding in pan-roasted chicken and store-bought gnocchi as Caprese’s newest co-stars.

Our one-pan creamy chicken and gnocchi is an all-time Delish favorite, but sometimes, you gotta try a few twists on a classic. Add Calabrian chile butter into the equation, and you might have just found your new favorite flavor combo.
